articles.title: In the Philippines, citizens are taking the lead in truth-telling
articles.description: The church and the civil society have set up a Truth Commission on the violent “war on drugs” unleashed by former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose trial begins at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on November 30.
paragraphs: In a shiny hall at the huge Pope Pius XII catholic center in Manila, the members of a Philippine Truth Commission are getting ready for the next public truth-telling session. In front of them sits Lorna Carina Pepaño, a lady with short greyish hair and glasses. In the middle of the room, a photo of her son, Christian Pepaño, is placed on a wooden chair. The picture shows him as a young, serious man, who looks straight into the camera. A branch of pink lilies near the picture is there to honor him.

On this day, October 9, 2026, Pepaño will tell the story of her beloved son, the life and violent death of her dear Christian. She is surrounded by women who came to support her. As the session will be broadcast, some are wearing face masks in order not to be recognized. One young woman has pulled up the hoody of her sweater. Next to Pepaño sits priest Flaviano Antonio Villanueva, well known for his support for victims of the “war on drugs”.

In 2016, Rodrigo Roa Duterte ran for president, promising that, if elected, he would act exactly as he did as mayor of Davao: in that city, he enforced a ruthless anti-drugs policy, established a death squad that liquidated addicts and dealers, while presenting those killings as a solution to societal problems and crimes. “Forget the laws on human rights,” he said. “If I make it to the presidential palace, I will do just what I did as mayor. You drug pushers, hold-up men, and do-nothings, you better get out because I’ll kill you.”

In predominantly catholic Philippines, more than 16 million people, including many priests and church leaders, voted for Duterte as their new president. Immediately after his installation, on July 1, 2016, Duterte launched his national “war on drugs”, called “Operation Double Barrel”, aimed at suppressing the use and sale of illegal drugs by cracking down on drug personalities and syndicates. Tortured and dead bodies were found on a daily basis in poor neighborhoods of Manila, the capital city.

This policy had two major components. “Operation Tokhang” tasked the police to knock on doors of the houses of suspected drugs users, runners and street pushers, to encourage them to stop, surrender and participate in rehabilitation programs. When people resisted, the order was: shoot to kill. Duterte even encouraged citizens to join in: “If you know of any addicts, go ahead and kill them yourself as getting their parents to do it would be too painful.” The second component was “Operation High Value Targets”, targeting suspected drug lords who have a higher-impact and allegedly corrupt local officials, such as mayors.

During Duterte’s term, from 2016 until 2022, according to official figures, police and hitmen of vigilante groups killed at least 6,250 people. However, civil society groups estimate that at least 30,000 people were extrajudicially executed in the Philippines. The vast majority were living in poor areas across the country.

Currently, Duterte is being prosecuted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague, in the Netherlands, where his trial starts on November 30, 2026. Meanwhile, in May 2026, the church and the civil society created the Philippine Truth Commission as a parallel and separate initiative.
articles.lede: The church and the civil society have set up a Truth Commission on the violent “war on drugs” unleashed by former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose trial begins at the International Criminal Court in The Hague on November 30.

articles.title: Beyond Only Intent
articles.description: [Dr. Gregory Stanton is Founding President of Genocide Watch, was Professor of Genocide Studies at George Mason University, President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and in t…
paragraphs: [ Dr. Gregory Stanton is Founding President of Genocide Watch, was Professor of Genocide Studies at George Mason University, President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and in the State Department drafted the UN Resolutions to create the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the Rules for the Khmer Rouge Tribunal.
Fitry Hamidah, Htet Htet Hliang, Anita Lesniak, Maximilian Millington, Emma Op het Veld, Tami Tasaki, Aymen Zehra, Natalie Kasper, and Omar Kausar are part of the Genocide Watch Legal Team.]

Article II of the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide ( Genocide Convention ), requires a determination that acts of genocide are committed by an individual or a state with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, as such.

Unlike other international crimes, the occurrence of one or more of the prohibited acts of genocide is not enough to prove commission of the crime of genocide. A disputing state accusing another state of violating the Genocide Convention must also prove that such acts were committed with the specific intent ( dolus specialis) to destroy a protected group.

Since evidence of genocidal intent is often not evident in statements by an individual or the leaders of a state, the ICTY, ICTR, and other international courts have recognized that intent to destroy a protected group may be inferred from patterns of conduct and the surrounding circumstances of actions.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007), the International Court of Justice (ICJ) held that, when genocidal intent is inferred from a pattern of conduct, the intent to destroy a group in whole or in part must be the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence. This doctrine has come to be known as the only intent test.

The Court repeated this test of intent in Croatia v. Serbia (2015). The only intent test sets a very high evidentiary threshold, making it almost impossible to prove genocidal intent to destroy a specific group. Especially for states, such specific intent usually coexists with military, political, or territorial intents.
The only intent test raises a crucial question: should the existence of another reasonable intent by a State automatically rule out genocidal intent?

To understand the ‘only reasonable inference’ standard, it is necessary to look at the laws of evidence in proving genocidal intent. The ICTR and ICTY only tried individuals, not states. These courts characterized the specific intent for genocide as “the conscious desire to achieve the destruction of the targeted group through the commission of the prohibited acts.” ( Akayesu, paras. 544-547; Kupreškić, para. 636; Krstić, para. 584).

Establishing specific intent to destroy a group presents considerable evidentiary challenges. Direct evidence or explicit manifestations of genocidal intent are rarely available ( Krstić Appeals, para. 32).
articles.lede: Fitry Hamidah, Htet Htet Hliang, Anita Lesniak, Maximilian Millington, Emma Op het Veld, Tami Tasaki, Aymen Zehra, Natalie Kasper, and Omar Kausar are part of the Genocide Watch Legal Team.]

articles.title: Electing the Fourth ICC Prosecutor: Preliminary Observations on the Process
articles.description: Introduction On 27 October 2026, the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties announced the procedure for electing the fourth Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court and published draft term…
paragraphs: On 27 October 2026, the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties announced the procedure for electing the fourth Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court and published draft terms of reference of an Advisory Committee and a vacancy announcement. According to an indicative timeline, applications close on 31 January 2027, and the election is to take place at the 26 th Session of the Assembly in December 2027 in The Hague, ‘unless the Bureau decides otherwise’. The Office of the Prosecutor will therefore have been without an elected head for at least 17 months after the removal of Karim Khan on 24 July 2026—an unprecedentedly long period without a principal of an organ in the Court’s history. To say that much is at stake in the upcoming elections would be an understatement. The procedure for the election of the next Prosecutor draws on lessons learnt from past experience and constitutes an improvement in several respects. However, it neglects the one lesson all three previous elections have taught. Political consultation, the key phase through which the Prosecutor is chosen, remains unregulated and unstructured, and this may defeat the purpose of the proposed procedure.

The first ICC Prosecutor, Luis Moreno Ocampo, was elected in April 2003 as the sole nominee, after months of informal consultations had produced a consensus candidate. In 2011, a Bureau Search Committee evaluated 51 candidates and shortlisted four. Ocampo’s Deputy Prosecutor, Fatou Bensouda, nominated by 66 States Parties, was elected by acclamation, although Article 42(4) Rome Statute requires a secret ballot. According to the Assembly’s evaluation, States were divided on nearly everything. Some considered that the Committee had added extra-statutory criteria and encroached on the right of States to nominate candidates. The Bureau conceded that it could present no conclusive recommendations (para 20).

In 2020, a Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor, assisted by a Panel of Experts, produced an unranked shortlist of four candidates. The Bureau’s ‘Way Forward’ of 13 November 2020 added five more, including Mr. Karim A. Khan. The troubled process ended with four failed rounds of consultations, and Khan was elected by secret ballot on 12 February 2021. The lessons-learnt report by the facilitators, drawing on separate reports of the former Presidency, the Committee, and the Panel, recorded the view of some States Parties that ‘politics, and lobbying, still played an influential role’ (para 104). The Justice Initiative’s review found that, although the terms of reference had been adopted more than 18 months before the vote, States began negotiating on actual candidates only weeks before it. Each election was decided by bypassing the agreed procedure—a tradition likely to continue this time around.

The Bureau deserves credit for improving the election procedure in at least three areas. First, vetting now precedes the assessment of candidates. All formally qualified candidates must undergo a due diligence check under a permanent procedure. An Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) confidential channel to communicate misconduct allegations will be open from 20 February to 20 April 2027, an IOM report will be due on 20 June, and interviews may take place only after the final report is received (draft terms of reference, para 10). That sequencing precludes the same failure that left the Advisory Committee on Nominations of Judges (ACN) unable, in its 2026 report, to make a conclusive determination on high moral character for any of the judicial candidates, having received only a preliminary IOM report. Second, a single candidate selection body—Advisory Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor (ACEP)—replaces the awkward pairing of Committee on the Election of the Prosecutor and the Panel of Experts, as many States had proposed with reference to the ACN model —an idea first floated in 2013. Third, there is a fixed end to consensus-building consultations among States, which a majority of States had requested, along with the publication of applications of the candidates the ACEP deems qualified and of the Committee’s report.

articles.title: Morocco / Western Sahara: Siege of Sahrawi human rights defender Sidi Mohamed Dadach's home and neighbourhood in El Aaiún
articles.description: MAR 003 / 1126 / OBS 058 Harassment / Intimidation / Restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly / Restrictions of the right to privacy / (…)
paragraphs: MAR 003 / 1126 / OBS 058 Harassment / Intimidation / Restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly / Restrictions of the right to privacy / Restrictions on freedom of movement Morocco / Western Sahara 16 November 2026

The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) and the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Western Sahara.

The Observatory has been informed of the ongoing surveillance and intimidation of Sahrawi human rights defender Mr Sidi Mohamed Dadach, President of the Committee for the Defence of the Right to Self-Determination for the People of Western Sahara (CODAPSO). He is also a former political prisoner who spent more than 24 years in detention and was awarded the Rafto Prize in recognition of his human rights activities in 2002.

On 28 October 2026, at approximately 5:15 p.m., a security operation was launched when Moroccan police surrounded Mr Dadach’s home in the aftermath of a meeting of the Coordination Mechanism for Sahrawi Human Rights Action. The security cordon extended across the entire Lirak neighbourhood, with security personnel deployed at its four entrances and around its perimeter. The operation involved police officers and local authority personnel, including individuals in civilian clothing, who were deployed at the four entrances to the Lirak neighbourhood and around its perimeter, where they monitored access to and movement within the neighbourhood.

The following day, on 29 October 2026, at approximately 8 p.m., two international observers, Marianne Bugge Stavik, a Norwegian national, and André Christopher Belleteste, a Norwegian-American national, were intercepted by six Moroccan police officers as they were returning to their hotel in El Aaiún. The officers reportedly told them that their presence in the city was unwelcome and instructed them to leave for Agadir. Both observers, 22-year-old university students studying in Norway, had met with Mr Dadach, other Sahrawi human rights defenders and relatives of Sahrawi political prisoners earlier that day. Their forced departure prevented them from completing their planned programme of meetings, including further exchanges with Sahrawi human rights defenders and families of political prisoners on 30 October 2026.

On 31 October 2026, the security siege imposed around Mr Dadach’s home in the Lirak neighbourhood of El Aaiún remained ongoing. Individuals whom he identified as local authority personnel wearing civilian clothing continued to monitor his movements and those of his family members, raising serious concerns regarding their safety, privacy and freedom of movement.

The Observatory recalls that it has repeatedly documented acts of surveillance, intimidation and restrictions on freedom of movement targeting Sahrawi human rights defenders in Western Sahara. In its statement of 31 July 2026, the Observatory reported renewed restrictions on movement, surveillance and intimidation targeting several members of the Collective of Sahrawi Human Rights Defenders (CODESA), including the continued siege and surveillance of the homes of its President, Ali Salem Tamek, and Vice-President Khadijetou Douih. In an earlier urgent appeal published on 28 February 2025, the Observatory also documented the siege and attack on the home of CODESA member Hassan Zerouali while international visitors were meeting with him to collect testimonies of human rights violations. These incidents illustrate a recurring pattern of surveillance and intimidation targeting Sahrawi human rights defenders in their homes and in connection with their legitimate human rights activities.

articles.title: The Weapon Passed Legal Review, Then the Software Changed
articles.description: For an AI-enabled weapon, the facts that matter most to a lawyer now live in software, not necessarily in hardware.
paragraphs: Every legal opinion rests on a statement of facts. A weapon’s legal review is no exception. Under U.S. Army Regulation (AR) 27-53, the program office that wants a weapon reviewed supplies a description of the system, its intended use, its anticipated effects, and the technical information behind them. The judge advocate’s opinion answers the question those facts pose. If the facts later change, the opinion does not become wrong. It becomes an opinion about a different weapon.

For most of the Army’s history, changing the facts meant changing the hardware, and changed hardware is hard to miss. Here, “software” includes executable code, trained artificial intelligence (AI) models and their weights, and the rules and parameter settings that govern the weapon’s behavior; it does not include physical hardware or live sensor observations. For an AI-enabled weapon, the facts that matter most to a lawyer now live in software: what the system treats as a target; how confident it must be before it acts; where it will and will not operate; and how much room a soldier has to stop it. Software of that kind is updated often, and an update leaves the launcher, the airframe, the serial number, and the name exactly as they were. This post is about the gap that opens when the legal review stays attached to the hardware while the facts move with the code, and about a short document that would close it.

Consider a hypothetical counter-drone interceptor that passed Army legal review before fielding. The review request described a system that detects small quadcopters, engages only inside a geofence (a boundary drawn in software beyond which the system will not act), fires only after a soldier confirms the target, and aborts within two seconds of a stop command. The opinion found the weapon lawful on those facts.

The first repairs a display fault. Engineers re-run the tests the weapon passed before fielding and confirm that target recognition, soldier confirmation, and the abort command behave as before. The facts in the review request are unchanged.

The second retrains the recognition model, the part of the software that decides what the sensors are looking at. After retraining, the weapon can also classify small fixed-wing aircraft as targets. Nothing about the launcher changed. The description of what the weapon identifies, which the opinion took as a given, has changed.

The third shortens a timing delay to make the system more responsive. It also has a side effect: the abort command now takes effect in four seconds, not two. The engineer who made the change recorded it as a performance fix.

A judge advocate would see at once that the second and third updates alter facts the opinion relied on, and that the third is the dangerous one, because nobody thought of it as a change to the weapon. The law can handle all three. The open question is whether anyone in the program will put the facts in front of a lawyer before the new version reaches the field.

AR 27-53 anticipates changed weapons. Paragraph 6f provides that if a fielded weapon is changed so that it is no longer the system or capability described in the review request, including a substantial change to its intended use or anticipated effects, the earlier review is no longer valid and a new review is required. Paragraph 6g addresses substantial changes in a weapon’s effects or accuracy. Paragraph 9 allows a program that is unsure whether review is required to put the question, through its servicing judge advocate, to the office The Judge Advocate General (TJAG) has designated for weapons reviews, ordinarily the National Security Law Division. The same paragraph bars fielding or employment of a weapon that needs a review and has not had one.
articles.lede: For an AI-enabled weapon, the facts that matter most to a lawyer now live in software, not necessarily in hardware.

Regret Is Not a Defence: The Assembly of States Parties and the Sanctioning of the International Criminal Court
articles.description: [Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez is an Adjunct Professor at the Pompeu Fabra Law Faculty, and a Senior Fellow at the Center for International Law Research and Policy. He is the author of Governing the In…
paragraphs: [ Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez is an Adjunct Professor at the Pompeu Fabra Law Faculty, and a Senior Fellow at the Center for International Law Research and Policy. He is the author of Governing the International Criminal Court: the History and Practice of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute (Brill, 2025).]

On 9 October 2026 the United States designated the International Criminal Court itself under Executive Order 14203. The general licence permitting dealings with the Court to be maintained or wound down expires on 7 April 2027, and the State Department has presented that window as time for States Parties to make progress on resolutions addressing United States concerns. The Bureau of the Assembly said it “regrets” the measure and called for its revocation, eight foreign ministers of States Parties declared themselves committed to “constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties” ahead of the 25th session of the Assembly of States Parties, which opens in The Hague on 30 November. One can understand the difficult position diplomats are in when it comes to defending the International Criminal Court from the United States, the superpower. Yet, if States Parties will not defend the institution besides political solidarity, then their governance role which equips them to act in tangible ways, is at risk of becoming irrelevant.

The Assembly is the Court’s international judicial governance institution, or injugovin. Article 112(2)(b), (d) and (g) confer on it management oversight, the budget and any other function consistent with the Statute. Together they ground what Bergsmo and others have called a “non-waivable duty of care” towards the institution States Parties created. The Assembly has said so much itself when in December 2025 it reaffirmed “the incompatibility of the consequences of coercive measures against the Court” with States Parties’ obligations under the Statute, the Agreement on Privileges and Immunities and the Headquarters Agreement. Having said so, it cannot treat the response against the United States and other non-State Parties like Russia as optional.

When Executive Order 14203 was signed in February 2025, 79 of 125 States Parties endorsed a joint statement of support. By October 2026, only 35 States Parties voiced some concern. Nonetheless, at its 24th session in 2025, the Assembly adopted by consensus a Declaration that names no State and “encourage[s] dialogue between States Parties and Non-States Parties”. The undisputed Declaration was adopted as the President of the Court explained to States Parties that nine elected officials, “ including one third of the Judges, as well as the totality of the ICC Presidency ,” were subject to Russian arrest warrants. Yet only the Declaration was passed as a political decision on the matter. A few days later, on 12 December 2025, the Moscow City Court convicted the Prosecutor and eight current and former judges in absentia, and on 8 October 2026 Russia sent extradition requests for all nine to the Netherlands and other States. The Presidency of the Assembly had responded to earlier Russian measures under its previous President. I have found no statement on the verdict or the requests by the current Presidency. By August 2026 the United States had designated nine of the eighteen judges, the President among them, both Deputy Prosecutors and the former Prosecutor. While much protective work is rightly confidential, it that does not explain why public texts and statements only speak of concern, regret and dialogue in the face of such blatant attack on the rule of law.
articles.lede: On 9 October 2026 the United States designated the International Criminal Court itself under Executive Order 14203.

articles.title: ‘Peace begins in our hearts’: Children close Muscat forum with a message to the world
articles.description: Children from across the world sent a message of peace from the Omani capital Muscat on Monday, calling for an end to hatred, respect for diversity and the protection of human rights.
paragraphs: Their message closed the two-day Muscat Plan of Action Forum, held on the International Day for Tolerance, marked by the UN every 16 November.

“Peace begins in our hearts, and in our belief that we all belong to one humanity,” the children said, describing understanding as the bridge between peoples and coexistence as the foundation for a safe and prosperous future.
They pledged to build bridges of solidarity, stand up for children’s rights, protect the planet and act as ambassadors for peace in their own communities.

On the forum’s second day, UN officials, religious and traditional leaders and experts discussed how to turn the goals of the Muscat Plan of Action – launched at UN Headquarters in New York in June – into practical programmes and partnerships.

Mohamed bin Said bin Khalfan Al Mamari, Oman’s Minister of Endowments and Religious Affairs, said the plan aims to strengthen the role of religious and traditional leaders and Indigenous Peoples in preventing conflict and combating hate speech.
“Difference in itself does not create conflict, just as similarity does not guarantee peace,” said Mr. Al Mamari.
Peace “is not merely the absence of violence or the cessation of conflicts and wars,” he continued, but needs a system built on justice, trust and security.
The minister called for stronger local mediators, a better link between early warning and institutional response and a bigger role for women and young people.

Chaloka Beyani, the UN Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide, said tolerance is the basis for peace, human rights and coexistence, warning that discrimination and exclusion can escalate into incitement to violence and crimes against humanity.
articles.lede: Children from across the world sent a message of peace from the Omani capital Muscat on Monday, calling for an end to hatred, respect for diversity and the protection of human rights.

articles.title: ICC: How far does a UN Security Council referral extend?
articles.description: In the Njeem case, the International Criminal Court has confirmed its jurisdiction over the situation in Libya. However, the judges were divided on the basis for jurisdiction. This is a sensitive debate that also concerns Sudan.
paragraphs: In a decision of November 2, 2026, a Pre-Trial Chamber of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unanimously confirmed its jurisdiction in the case concerning Osama Elmasry Njeem, also known as Osama Almasri Njeem. This unanimity, however, masks a significant divergence of opinion amongst the judges. For Judges Iulia Antoanella Motoc and Reine Alapini-Gansou, the crimes with which Njeem is charged fall within the Court’s jurisdiction because they remain covered by the United Nations Security Council’s 2011 referral of the situation in Libya. Judge María del Socorro Flores Liera, on the other hand, deemed that the Court’s jurisdiction is based on a declaration submitted by Libya in 2025.
This divergence fuels a sensitive debate, which also concerns Sudan: how long can a Security Council referral remain in force?

On February 26, 2011, whilst Muammar Gaddafi’s regime was violently suppressing a popular uprising in Libya, the Security Council adopted Resolution 1970. Acting under Chapter VII of the United Nations Charter, it decided to refer to the ICC Prosecutor “the situation in the Libyan Arab Jamahiriya since 15 February 2011”.

This referral had a key distinguishing feature: Libya was not – and still is not – a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. The Court’s jurisdiction was therefore not based on ratification of the Statute by the State concerned, but on a provision of the Statute itself allowing the Security Council to refer a situation to the Prosecutor.

In this context, a Pre-Trial Chamber issued an arrest warrant for Njeem on January, 18, 2025. He is suspected of having run detention centres in Tripoli in which thousands of people have allegedly been detained for long periods. The warrant relates to war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, acts of torture, cruel treatment, rape and other sexual violence, as well as acts of imprisonment and persecution committed at Mitiga prison from February, 15, 2015 onwards.

According to the prosecution, these crimes were committed personally by Njeem, on his orders or with his assistance, and by members of the Special Deterrence Force, also known as SDF/RADA. The victims were reportedly detained on religious grounds, due to their alleged opposition to the ideology of SDF/RADA or their alleged links with other armed groups.

Arrested in Turin, Italy, on January 19, 2025, Njeem was released and returned to Libya two days later by the Italian authorities, under highly controversial circumstances. This led the ICC to find that Italy had breached its obligations to cooperate, and to refer the matter to the Assembly of States Parties, which is due to consider this issue at its next session from November 30 to December 7, 2026, in The Hague.

The defence contested both the ICC’s jurisdiction and the admissibility of the case. In its view, Resolution 1970 relates to a specific crisis: the violence committed in 2011 by the state apparatus of the Gaddafi regime. The acts of which Njeem is accused, committed several years later in a different political and institutional context, do not, it argued, have a sufficient link to that initial situation.
articles.lede: In the Njeem case, the International Criminal Court has confirmed its jurisdiction over the situation in Libya. However, the judges were divided on the basis for jurisdiction.

articles.title: International Law for a Fragile World: Political Risk – Authoritarianism, Information Warfare, and Democratic Fragility (Part II)
articles.description: [Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).] Part I of this post argued…
paragraphs: [ Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).]

Part I of this post argued that contemporary democratic decline proceeds less through dramatic ruptures than through the cumulative, often formally lawful erosion of the institutions that allow political systems to correct themselves, and that international law – organised around discrete rights and flagrant violations – struggles to perceive this process until it is far advanced. This second part examines the dimension of political fragility that has been most profoundly transformed by technology – the information environment – before turning to the paradox that confronts democracies seeking to defend themselves, and to the elements of a legal approach capable of governing political risk before the threshold of irreversibility is crossed.

Propaganda and political manipulation are not new. States have always sought to influence foreign publics, and political actors have always deployed misleading claims. What has changed is the architecture through which influence operates. Digital platforms permit political communication at unprecedented scale and speed; recommender systems amplify emotionally provocative material irrespective of its accuracy; generative artificial intelligence has collapsed the cost of producing persuasive synthetic text, images, audio, and video; networks of inauthentic accounts allow narratives to be repeated across platforms until they acquire the appearance of consensus; and microtargeting fragments political communication so that different citizens encounter different versions of political reality. Foreign operations need not create domestic divisions – they exploit and amplify those that already exist.

Recent practice illustrates the range of techniques. In September 2024, the United States Department of Justice seized 32 internet domains used by the so-called “Doppelganger” operation, run by Russian companies acting at the direction of the Presidential Administration, which cloned the websites of established news outlets to disseminate fabricated articles and amplified them through influencers and paid social media advertising. Two days before Slovakia’s parliamentary elections in September 2023 – during the legally mandated pre-election moratorium on campaigning – an AI-generated audio recording purporting to capture the leader of a liberal opposition party discussing electoral fraud with a journalist circulated widely, at a moment when neither the media nor the parties concerned could effectively respond. In Moldova, the OSCE/ODIHR observation mission to the 2024 presidential election and constitutional referendum on European integration found that contestants campaigned freely “despite concerns over illicit foreign interference and active disinformation efforts”, and called for stronger action against vote-buying and illicit campaign finance – practices that national authorities attributed to a network directed from Russia. Information manipulation, financial inducements, and the exploitation of distrust are no longer separate techniques but components of integrated campaigns.

articles.title: International Law for a Fragile World: Political Risk – Authoritarianism, Information Warfare, and Democratic Fragility (Part I)
articles.description: [Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).] The preceding posts in thi…
paragraphs: [ Dr Sergey Sayapin is Visiting Principal Research Fellow at the NUS Centre for International Law and Professor of Law at KIMEP University (Almaty, Kazakhstan; on leave).]

The preceding posts in this series have examined fragility in ecological, technological, human, and economic systems. All of these forms of risk, however, converge upon a further system whose resilience international law has largely taken for granted: the political institutions through which societies decide how every other risk is to be governed. Climate adaptation requires governments capable of planning beyond the electoral cycle; pandemic preparedness depends upon public trust in credible institutions; technological governance presupposes authorities able to regulate powerful private actors; and economic resilience requires governments capable of making contested distributive choices under uncertainty. When political institutions themselves become fragile, the capacity to govern every other category of risk deteriorates with them. Democratic erosion should therefore be understood not merely as a problem of constitutional design or domestic political organisation but as a form of systemic risk – and, in a sense, as the meta-risk of a fragile world.

The empirical evidence is difficult to dismiss. Freedom House reported in March 2026 that global freedom declined in 2025 for the twentieth consecutive year, with 54 countries deteriorating and only 35 improving; the share of the world’s population living in countries rated “Free” has fallen from 46 to 21 per cent in two decades. International IDEA’s Global State of Democracy 2025 found that 94 of the 173 countries it assesses – 54 per cent – had declined in at least one key dimension of democratic performance compared with five years earlier, that its indicator of credible elections had fallen to its lowest level in thirty years, and that press freedom had suffered its most far-reaching decline since the dataset began in 1975. The V-Dem Institute’s Democracy Report 2026 counts 92 autocracies against 87 democracies and estimates that almost three-quarters of humanity now lives under autocratic rule. These assessments differ in method, but they converge on a single conclusion: decline is no longer confined to fragile or transitional states. It is a structural feature of the contemporary international order.

This two-part post argues that international law is insufficiently equipped to understand this phenomenon because it protects democracy primarily through individual rights, electoral standards, and the prohibition of unlawful external interference. These protections remain indispensable. Yet democratic fragility increasingly develops through processes that are cumulative rather than episodic, informational rather than territorial, and frequently lawful when each measure is considered in isolation. Part I examines how democratic erosion operates and why the architecture of international law struggles to capture it. Part II turns to information warfare, the paradox of democratic self-defence, and the contours of a legal approach to democratic risk governance.
articles.lede: The preceding posts in this series have examined fragility in ecological, technological, human, and economic systems.

articles.title: Pre-Trial Chamber II of the ICC Closes (or Attempts to Close?) the Afghanistan Investigation
articles.description: In our previous post, we discussed a curious set of procedural developments at the International Criminal Court (ICC), with Pre-Trial Chamber II (the PTC) ordering the Prosecution to open a second …
paragraphs: In our previous post, we discussed a curious set of procedural developments at the International Criminal Court (ICC), with Pre-Trial Chamber II (the PTC) ordering the Prosecution to open a second investigation in relation to the Situation in Afghanistan. The PTC also ordered the transfer of court records, including the four arrest warrants it had already issued within the ambit of the ongoing investigation, to the new ‘Situation in Afghanistan II’. We noted too that the PTC appeared to act on its own initiative, without any basis in the Court’s statutory framework, and without submissions from the Prosecution or anyone else. The Prosecution has appealed both decisions; these appeals are currently pending before the Appeals Chamber (AC). In the meantime, and seemingly without heed to the ongoing appeals, the PTC has now, on 12 November 2026, ordered the closure of the ongoing investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan. With that, as captured in immediate reporting, is the closure of any ‘ investigation into US war crimes in Afghanistan ,’ among other alleged crimes, including by Islamic State.

The best that can be said of the latest decision is that it at least makes clear what was driving the initial, procedurally irregular, decision to split the ongoing investigation into two. The latest decision asserts a motivation of securing ‘the objectives of legal certainty, transparency and the proper administration of judicial proceedings’ (para 22). The pursuit of these values is difficult to take at face value. After setting out the PTC’s reasoning, we raise technical, institutional, and strategic difficulties with the decision.

As a starting point, Pre-Trial Chamber II again invokes its own ‘inherent judicial powers’, which it proposes are necessary to ‘safeguard the fairness and legality of the proceedings’ (para 14). This aside, the legal basis suggested by the Chamber is Regulation 66 ter (2) of the Regulations of Court, adopted by the Court’s judges. Notably, Regulation 66 ter, which addresses the ‘[c]losure and reopening of case and situation records’, was included in the Regulations by way of amendment less than a month before the PTC’s decision to split the Situation in Afghanistan in two. The Regulation states, in the relevant part:

(a) When the Prosecutor, having provided information in accordance with regulation 45, sub-regulation 1, decides not to initiate an investigation, or determines that he or she does not anticipate any further investigatory or prosecutorial activities in a situation in relation to which an investigation has been initiated, he or she shall inform in writing the Pre-Trial Chamber to which the situation has been assigned.

(b) Having been so informed, the Pre-Trial Chamber may, upon application or proprio motu, order the Registrar, when appropriate, to close the record of the situation. The Pre-Trial Chamber shall be responsible for judicial matters of a residual nature in this situation, unless otherwise provided in the Statute, the Rules or these Regulations or such matters are assigned to another Chamber by the Presidency.

articles.title: Two Weeks in Review: 2—13 November 2026
articles.description: Over the last two weeks, it is chiefly the institutions of international law that have been in focus. There have been a number of responses to the judicial elections at the International Court of J…
paragraphs: Over the last two weeks, it is chiefly the institutions of international law that have been in focus. There have been a number of responses to the judicial elections at the International Court of Justice, from congratulations to the incoming benchers, to consternation at the growing disparity in global representation, and a look forward to the election of the President next year. Commentators have also turned to the ICC’s decision to split the Afghanistan investigation, and the UN Security Council’s failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate in Western Sahara. Meanwhile, State practice following the recognition of Palestine has raised problems concerning Palestinian nationality and statelessness, in particular the protections for Palestinians under international law. And the updated ICRC Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention continues to struggle to address fully persons with disabilities. Not to mention a critical look at EJIL’s AI policy, and the use of the global carbon budget in climate litigation before domestic courts.
Marko Milanovic congratulates EJIL:Talk’s very own Dapo Akande on his election to the International Court of Justice—replete with AI-generated video laudatio.

Eric Chan turns our attention from who is in, to who is out. The United Kingdom may have regained a seat, restoring representation of all five permanent Security Council members, but the elections have left Latin America and the Caribbean with only one judge for the first time in the Court’s history. Take a look at voting patterns in the General Assembly and Security Council, and this outcome illustrates the tensions between informal regional seat allocations, the privileged position of the P5, and the requirement under Article 9 of the ICJ Statute to represent the world’s principal legal systems and forms of civilisation. This raises a deeper question, whether preserving established patterns of representation adequately reflects the diversity of international legal traditions—particularly given the historical contributions and contemporary under-representation of the Global South.

And looking ahead, Noam Morris examines the forthcoming February 2027 election of the ICJ’s President and Vice-President, distinguishing the President’s institutional and diplomatic responsibilities from their procedural and judicial functions under Article 21 of the ICJ Statute and the Court’s Rules. Drawing on historical election patterns, he identifies the influence of judicial seniority, re-election cycles, geographical representation, and gender diversity on the selection of the Court’s leadership. The growing complexity and political sensitivity of the Court’s docket make judicial experience, administrative competence, diplomatic skill, and the ability to manage deliberations especially important considerations in the election.

Miles Jackson and Priya Urs criticise the ICC Pre-Trial Chamber’s decision to require a separate investigation into crimes committed against women and girls following the Taliban’s return to power in 2021, notwithstanding existing arrest warrants issued within the Afghanistan situation. They question the Chamber’s reliance on inherent judicial oversight powers under Articles 15 and 53 of the Rome Statute, arguing that its intervention lacks a clear statutory basis, contradicts the Appeals Chamber’s approach to the scope of investigations, and creates uncertainty over the validity and jurisdictional basis of existing warrants. The decision risks undermining prosecutorial independence under Article 42, introducing procedural inconsistency and delaying justice for victims.

articles.title: London Calling: The Customary Law of Naval Blockade and Contemporary Practice
articles.description: The employment of naval blockades in recent conflicts confirms that States continue to view them as an important method of warfare.
paragraphs: Naval blockade has long occupied a distinctive place within the law of naval warfare. Until very recently some commentators regarded it as a relic of an earlier era, however, the employment of naval blockades in recent conflicts has confirmed that States continue to view them as an important method of warfare. Although the fundamental principles of blockade law were set out in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, notably in the 1856 Declaration of Paris and the 1909 London Declaration Concerning the Laws of Naval War (which States never ratified and therefore never entered into force), its legal foundation has always rested principally upon customary international law. The classical requirements that a blockade be declared, notified, effective, impartial in its application, and respectful of access to neutral ports have remained remarkably stable for more than a century. These core criteria have been consistently reaffirmed in naval manuals and, more importantly, reflected in State practice.

Nevertheless, the use, and potential abuse, of blockade in situations where vulnerable civilian populations may face harm has led human rights advocates, humanitarian organizations, and some legal scholars to question whether blockade, in its current form, is compatible with contemporary international humanitarian law. The expression of such humanitarian concerns raises a fundamental question about the current state of blockade: does contemporary State practice confirm the validity of the customary law of blockade, as reflected in the 1909 London Declaration, or does it indicate that the Declaration’s traditional requirement of effectiveness is being reshaped by modern humanitarian norms?

This post argues that contemporary maritime practice demonstrates that the essential legal characteristics of blockade, as outlined in the 1909 London Declaration, have neither been abandoned nor transformed; rather, recent conflicts reveal a remarkable continuity in the customary law of blockade. States continue to declare blockades, enforce them through naval, air and other assets, intercept neutral shipping, and justify such measures by reference to established principles of the law of naval warfare. That which has changed is not the belligerent right to conduct naval blockades but rather the broader legal environment within which the law of naval blockade exists.

Naval blockade is a distinct belligerent maritime operation intended to prevent vessel traffic from all States from entering or leaving specified coastal areas that are under the sovereignty, occupation, or control of an enemy. Such areas may include ports and harbors, the entire coastline, or parts of it. As a distinct operation, it is governed by a body of rules that have evolved over five centuries and has been shaped through the practice of maritime powers, interpreted and refined by the jurisprudence of prize courts, and accepted as part of the belligerent right to wage war at sea.

Historically, blockade emerged from the broader doctrine that a belligerent was entitled to deny an adversary the use of the sea for military and economic purposes. By the late eighteenth century, British and American prize courts had recognized blockade as a lawful means of warfare, so long as certain minimum conditions were satisfied. These conditions reflected a balance between the legitimate military interests of belligerents and the rights of neutral States to engage in maritime commerce.
articles.lede: The employment of naval blockades in recent conflicts confirms that States continue to view them as an important method of warfare.

articles.title: Genocide and Myanmar at ICJ
articles.description: “It’s the World Court and it’s genocide: you don’t really get any bigger than that especially when it comes from reporting in The Hague,” says Stephanie van den Berg, cohost of our podcast partners at Asymmetrical Haircuts.
paragraphs: On 19 November the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will be ruling in a really significant case against the government of Myanmar, which is accused of committing genocide ‌against the minority Muslim Rohingya. Gambia brought the case to the ICJ under the Genocide Convention in 2019. During the hearings Gambia argued that ⁠a 2017 offensive by Myanmar government forces that forced at least 730,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh constituted a genocide. Myanmar denies the charge and has said the offensive was a counter-terrorism campaign and therefore legitimate and definitely not genocide.

It’s the first time the UN court may rule that a state is liable for genocide. Melanie O’Brien, Professor of International Law at the University of Western Australia Law School and former President of the International Association of Genocide Scholars explains the challenging legal issues that make this case so important in the field of international justice.
articles.lede: “It’s the World Court and it’s genocide: you don’t really get any bigger than that especially when it comes from reporting in The Hague,” says Stephanie van den Berg, cohost of our podcast partners at Asymmetrical Haircuts.

articles.title: In the digital realm of the “RD4U”
articles.description: The Register of damages caused by Russia in Ukraine – also known as RD4U – has begun to operate. It has already received about 200,000 claims. Its executive director explains its current operations and future hopes.
paragraphs: With a Star Wars style acronym – RD4U – the ‘Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation Against Ukraine’, to give it its official name, is now completely open for business. All 43 categories of claims for compensation for “damage, loss or injury caused by the internationally wrongful acts of the Russian Federation in or against Ukraine, starting on or after 24 February 2022” can now be submitted by individuals, companies or the state of Ukraine.

The Register started in April 2024 and is part of a complex interconnected set of structures including a ‘Claims Commission’ which – when it gets the ratifications needed from states – will subsume the Register into itself as one component, and continue to process claims, then adjudicate upon them, while waiting for the final cog in the machine to be added: a payment system.

There’s little comparison with other claims mechanisms developed by treaty over the years, except maybe for scale, the UN Compensation Commission that dealt with post Iraq invasion of Kuwait processing more than 2 million claims over 11 years. This one has been built at rapid speed. Distinctively, it was created during the hostilities rather than after and operates digitally via app.

“It's one of the maybe underappreciated aspects of our work,” says the Register executive director Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi. “We don't have a precedent to rely on for how to build a mechanism while the war not only is ongoing, but in many ways is as intense as at any point in the past almost 5 years.” The different challenges include availability of documentation, and the fact that “some evidence is simply lost,” he notes. “It's already becoming, at times, difficult to reconstruct events in the beginning of the war in 2022. So, from that perspective, I feel quite justified that we have started work early.”

The RD4U is based in The Hague, where so much of the old and new architecture of international justice is being created. It is completely separate from the new Special Tribunal on Aggression against Ukraine, “politically and virtually in any other way,” stresses Kliuchkovskyi. “They have different mandates, different purposes, different memberships.” He acknowledges that both are “under the Council of Europe umbrella” and in The Hague. But the special tribunal “is a mechanism for individual criminal liability, whereas the compensation mechanism, including the register, is meant to pursue state liability for violations of international law”.

Kliuchkovskyi sits in a small office in the international zone of the Dutch city, a stone's throw from Europol, Eurojust, and the former premises of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. As we comment on the blandness of the furniture visible in the zoom chat, he replies: “I don't know if it's IKEA. We inherited it from the previous landlord in this space, and we haven't bothered to change it, because that's all we need. Our physical presence is kept lean on purpose. As we semi-joke, our magic happens in the digital realm.”
articles.lede: The Register of damages caused by Russia in Ukraine – also known as RD4U – has begun to operate. It has already received about 200,000 claims.

articles.title: Splitting the ICC’s Afghanistan Investigation: Judicial Oversight or Overreach?
articles.description: On 5 October 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed four warrants of arrest against senior Taliban leaders in the Situation in Afghanistan. The warrants, whic…
paragraphs: On 5 October 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed four warrants of arrest against senior Taliban leaders in the Situation in Afghanistan. The warrants, which were initially issued under seal on 8 July 2025 and 9 September 2025, concern the charge of gender persecution as a crime against humanity under Article 7(1)(h) of the Rome Statute. In substance, they alleged the severe deprivation, ‘through decrees and edicts, [of] girls and women of the rights to education, privacy and family life and the freedoms of movement, expression, thought, conscience and religion’, as well as the targeting of others ‘because certain expressions of sexuality and/or gender identity…’ The charges, and the identities of the suspects, raise novel issues of considerable importance, some of which have already been addressed in commentary.

At the same time, a set of curious procedural developments in the Situation in Afghanistan has received far less attention. On 15 July 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II ordered the Prosecution to open a separate investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan concerning ‘crimes committed against women and girls after the Taliban takeover in 2021’ (para 6). This decision, which was initially issued under seal and available only to the Prosecution, appears to have been issued by the Pre-Trial Chamber (PTC) unbidden; that is, acting on its own initiative and without submissions from the Prosecution (or anyone else). This post addresses some questionable aspects of the PTC’s decision, including the fact that the very same Chamber has already issued four arrest warrants in relation to cases arising out of the existing Situation in Afghanistan, all of which pertain to crimes allegedly committed by members of the Taliban government since 2021.
We do not recount in detail the complex history of the Situation in Afghanistan here. For present purposes, it is sufficient to note:
As noted above, there are now four public arrest warrants, all of which concern the conduct of senior Taliban leaders since 2021.

In its decision of 15 July 2026, the PTC directed the Prosecution, ‘should it continue to consider that the requirements of article 53(1) of the Statute are met, to open a new investigation on the basis of the Referral submitted by the six States Parties on 28 November 2024’. The Chamber considered that the ‘principle of judicial oversight’ in relation to investigations authorised under Article 15(4), such as the ongoing investigation in Afghanistan, imposed upon it ‘an inherent responsibility to ensure that investigations … remain within the scope authorised by the Court’ (para 10).

As to the situation in Afghanistan, the Chamber explained that it was necessary to examine ‘whether, having regard to the particular features of the conduct described in the Referral, those allegations should be addressed within the existing investigation into the Situation in Afghanistan or in a separate investigation’ (para 10). The Taliban takeover of 2021 was a ‘materially different factual and institutional context, involv[ing] distinct modes of commission’, with the relevant allegations being unrelated to any armed conflict (para 14). In the Chamber’s view, the new referral ‘concerns allegations of gender and political persecution through the adoption, implementation and enforcement of discriminatory decrees, policies and restrictions made possible by the Taliban’s exercise of de facto governmental authority, rather than conduct allegedly committed by the Taliban as an insurgent armed group during the armed conflict’ (para 14). The ‘proper administration of justice and the orderly management of the Court’s proceedings’ justified a separate and new investigation.
articles.lede: On 5 October 2026, Pre-Trial Chamber II of the International Criminal Court (ICC) unsealed four warrants of arrest against senior Taliban leaders in the Situation in Afghanistan.

Haiti: More than 1,000 killed between July and September, UN report reveals
articles.description: More than 1,000 people were killed in Haiti during the third quarter of this year, as armed gangs continue to terrorize the population in the capital Port-au-Prince and beyond, the UN team in the island nation, said in its latest human rights report.
paragraphs: It details bloody turf wars, sexual violence and other horrors, noting that serious violations and abuses continue to be committed across the Port-au-Prince metropolitan area and in the Artibonite and South-East departments.

“The scale of the massacres documented during this period, particularly in Kenscoff and several other localities that had previously been spared, reminds us of the absolute need to strengthen both mechanisms for protecting the population and the presence of the State in recently liberated areas,” said Carlos Ruiz Massieu, Special Representative of the UN Secretary-General in Haiti and Head of the UN Integrated Office in the country, BINUH.
The UN Security Council has authorized a Gang Suppression Force for the Caribbean country which has yet to be fully deployed.

Between July and September, at least 1,167 people were killed and 459 injured in Haiti. Gangs were responsible for more than 45 per cent of these incidents, while around five per cent were attributable to self-defence groups targeting gang members and people suspected of collaborating with them.

The report notes that more than half of all documented killings and injuries occurred during ground or aerial operations carried out by security forces against gangs, sometimes with the support of a private military company using drones.

Armed groups maintained a grip on neighbourhoods in the capital under their control, carrying out targeted killings in retaliation for security operations. They also murdered people who refused to be extorted, respect their rules or who had denounced attempts by gang leaders to interfere in the electoral process.

Gang members who had been driven out of neighbourhoods such as Bel Air and La Saline by security operations earlier in the year gradually regained a foothold in these areas and committed further abuses there.

In early August, gangs beheaded at least 19 people in the Cité Soleil neighbourhood, including 12 elderly women. Two attacks in the town of Kenscoff in July and August left at least 105 people dead, including 19 children. More than 36 victims were shot dead in the courtyard of a Protestant church.
Attacks were also carried out in the communes of Saint-Michel-de-l’Attalaye in Artibonite and Marigot in South-East, areas that had previously been largely spared from gang infiltration.

articles.title: Regulating ‘Killer Robots’: another missed opportunity?
articles.description: On 16-20 November in Geneva States will deliberate on what could form the basis of a future Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) instrument. But what does this mean for civilian protection and meeting the challenges of algorithmic warfare?
paragraphs: One glance at recent headlines on automated and accelerated decision-making in targeting in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and elsewhere, shows how far the time required for doubt, reflection – and human witnessing – has been stripped, without a corresponding emphasis on understanding and accounting for what is lost for civilians forced to exist and survive in these conflicts.

Over the past two decades, artificial intelligence (AI) in the military domain, which includes a reliance on algorithmic decision-support systems and predictive pattern-of-life targeting, has dramatically altered how war is experienced, and how crucial parts of International Humanitarian Law (IHL) – such as civilian status – are interpreted.

In early September 2026, the final meeting of the United Nations group of governmental experts (GGE) on emerging technologies in the area of Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems concluded a final text of “elements for an instrument”, adopted by states, available to read online. The text will be presented to delegations convening in Geneva, the Swiss capital of diplomacy, at the seventh review conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons – commonly referred to as the ‘CCW’ – which will be held this month from 16 to 20th November 2026.

A reading of the text – often referred to as “regulating killer robots” – generates a disturbing disconnect from the reality of today’s wars and raises questions about whether a treaty in this forum could ever serve to restrain autonomous or artificial intelligence-assisted uses of force.

The 1980 CCW is an international treaty banning or restricting the use of weapons considered to cause unnecessary or unjustifiable suffering to combatants and indiscriminate harm to civilians, in both international and non-international armed conflicts. It operates through five annexed protocols, designed to be added to, which address specific categories of harmful weapons:

Could there be a sixth protocol on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (also known by the acronym LAWS)? Possibly. The CCW was designed to be a flexible convention, so new weapons protocols could be added to it over time. Under article 8 of the CCW, any state that has ratified the treaty has the power to propose an additional protocol relating to categories of conventional weapons not yet covered, and a conference to negotiate a protocol can proceed if a majority of states agree. Or, states can collectively decide on new protocol negotiations at a meeting.

Because the CCW operates by consensus, a decision can only be made if no member state actively objects to it. This enables broad participation on the one hand, but on the other hand means that the CCW requires the passive or explicit agreement of every single participating state, which has implications for how text is negotiated – vetoed and blocked, or compromised and diluted. Some states embrace consensus and others instrumentalise it, diluting the collective will and ambition, as Yvette Issar from the Quaker UN Office in Geneva, has reflected on.
articles.lede: On 16-20 November in Geneva States will deliberate on what could form the basis of a future Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) instrument.

articles.title: A collective step forward: the outcome document on achieving meaningful protection for hospitals in armed conflict
cats: Upholding humanity in war: the Global IHL Initiative
articles.description: When war reaches hospitals, protection becomes a matter of life and death. Discover what international humanitarian law demands.
paragraphs: Hospitals and other medical facilities enjoy specific protection under international humanitarian law (IHL), yet the reality in contemporary armed conflicts is starkly different. Attacks against health-care facilities, their misuse and impediments to their functioning continue to put patients and medical personnel at risk and undermine access to essential medical care. Against this backdrop, more than 100 states from all regions came together through the Global IHL Initiative to examine what meaningful protection for medical facilities requires in practice.

In this post, ICRC Legal Advisers Supriya Rao and Alexander Breitegger examine the recently released outcome document on Achieving Meaningful Protection for Medical Facilities in Conflict, resulting from several rounds of consultations with states led by Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain, Uruguay and the ICRC. This piece highlights key parts from the outcome document, including what the specific protection afforded to medical facilities entails, the strict conditions under which that protection may be lost, and the rules that continue to constrain attacks even when it is lost. Drawing on two years of state consultations and expert discussions, it also considers areas of disagreement among states and explains how the positions reflected in the outcome document can help states translate their existing legal obligations into meaningful protection on the ground.

Hospitals and other medical facilities enjoy one of the highest levels of protection under international humanitarian law (IHL), reflecting their life-saving function and going beyond the protection enjoyed by other civilian objects. Yet there is a widening gap between the protection the law provides and the grim reality on the ground, as attacks against health-care facilities, their misuse and impediments to their functioning continue to take a devastating toll. It was in response to this gap that the protection of medical facilities was chosen as one of the workstreams of the Global IHL Initiative.

Led by four co-chairing states – Nigeria, Pakistan, Spain and Uruguay – together with the ICRC, the workstream sought to reaffirm and deepen understanding of the existing IHL rules protecting medical facilities in contemporary armed conflict. It also aimed to identify practical measures, drawing on existing law and good practices from states, to strengthen implementation of those rules. The resulting outcome document, Achieving Meaningful Protection for Medical Facilities in Conflict, does not seek to create new law and is not open for endorsement. It reflects five consultations with more than 100 participating states from all regions of the world over 18 months, complemented by two expert workshops bringing together a wealth of experience and expertise.

At a time when hospitals are increasingly targeted or otherwise affected by hostilities, the outcome document provides an important reaffirmation of the specific protection IHL affords medical facilities. It examines what that protection requires in practice and offers states a concrete tool for translating their legal obligations into meaningful protection on the ground. In doing so, it demonstrates that respecting and protecting medical facilities during armed conflict is both possible and essential to fulfilling the fundamental obligation to care for the wounded and sick. It may also contribute to countering narratives and interpretations that portray the IHL rules protecting hospitals as significantly more flexible than they actually are.
articles.lede: When war reaches hospitals, protection becomes a matter of life and death. Discover what international humanitarian law demands.

Fair Share Obligations in Climate Change Litigation: Towards a Global Carbon Approach?
articles.description: In January of this year, the District Court of The Hague’s first-instance decision in Bonaire v The Netherlands found the Netherlands to be in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convent…
paragraphs: In January of this year, the District Court of The Hague’s first-instance decision in Bonaire v The Netherlands found the Netherlands to be in violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the European Convention of Human Rights (“ECHR”) for failing to take sufficient climate mitigation and adaptation measures, resulting in discrimination towards the inhabitants of Bonaire.

Bonaire is among an increasing number of domestic court decisions that interpret human and constitutional rights in light of the international climate treaties to require each State to play their “part” or contribute their “fair share” in the mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions. Such language has its origins in the early Urgenda decision of 2019, which first put forward the concept of “partial responsibility” in the context of emission reductions: “each country is responsible for its part and can therefore be called to account in that respect” (para. 5.7.5). In adopting such logic, domestic courts globally reject the drop in the ocean argument in which individual responsibility for climate harm is diluted merely because emissions are cumulative in nature ( see decisions in Australia, Belgium, Germany, and Korea ).

While still under appeal, the District Court in Bonaire took this reasoning a step further. In its assessment of Article 8 of the ECHR, the District Court considered it a negative factor that the Netherlands had not quantified its emission allowance based on the remaining global carbon budget to limit global warming to 1.5°C (para. 11.15). In assessing whether the Netherlands had sufficiently played its part in emission reductions, it endorsed a global carbon budget approach.

This post draws attention to an increasing number of domestic courts that hold governments accountable for their failure to quantify their “fair share” of emissions in line with the global carbon budget. The first part defines the global carbon budget approach with reference to the reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (“IPCC”). The second unpacks the legal reasoning of recent domestic and regional court decisions that require States to determine their “fair share” on this basis. The third examines domestic courts’ engagement with the best available science to determine methodological considerations for calculating their “fair share” of emissions apportioned to the global carbon budget. It thereby points to an emerging practice of establishing responsibility for States’ due diligence obligations to reduce emissions commensurate with global mitigation efforts and fairness considerations, without necessarily evidencing a direct causal nexus with environmental harm.

The IPCC has estimated with a 50% probability that to keep greenhouse gas emission reductions in line with the 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, only 500 GtCO 2 remains available to be released into the atmosphere from 1 st January 2020 (p. 678). Under the global carbon budget approach, States collectively had a finite quantity of CO 2 in 2020 – exactly 500 GtCO 2 – that can be used in the transition to net-zero by 2050. Thus, for a State to contribute its “fair share”, it must carve out its share of remaining emissions from the global carbon budget consistently with its obligations under the international climate change regime, such as the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities (“CBDR”) and set emission reduction targets accordingly.

articles.title: Mind the Gap: The Distance Between WHO Data and International Legal Standards
articles.description: Recent report concludes that WHO attack data cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it.
paragraphs: International lawyers, UN bodies, and human rights organizations increasingly cite one source when they discuss violence against health care in armed conflict: the World Health Organization’s Surveillance System on Attacks on Health Care (SSA). Since its launch in 2017, the SSA has become the default empirical basis for claims about the scale and pattern of harm caused to hospitals, clinics, medical transport, and health personnel in dozens of conflicts. The UN Office of the Special Representative for the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict draws on it. Special rapporteurs cite it. Advocacy organizations build their own datasets on top of it. It now shapes the narrative of accountability for alleged attacks on health care and forms the basis for misplaced arguments about culpability for them as breaches of international humanitarian standards.

We spent months reviewing the SSA’s methodology and publicly available data. Our conclusion—in a report recently published by The Hague Initiative for International Cooperation and the Henry Jackson Society—is that the system, as currently designed, cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it. This is not an argument against monitoring attacks on health care, which is an important and legitimate project. It is an argument that continuing to treat SSA figures as verified, comparable, or legally dispositive risks distorting the debate it’s meant to inform.

The SSA defines an “attack” as “any act of verbal or physical violence, threat of violence or other psychological violence, or obstruction that interferes with the availability, access and delivery of curative and/or preventive health services.” This is considerably broader than the operative legal definition of “attack” found in Additional Protocol I, Article 49, which requires an “act of violence against the adversary” connected to an armed conflict.

The over-extension matters. The SSA’s event taxonomy includes categories such as “psychological” violence (insults, intimidation, threats) and “obstruction,” which by the WHO’s own methodology can include a health worker being delayed at a security checkpoint, which is not an “act of violence.” It also includes arrests, detentions, and searches; categories of State and non-State conduct that international humanitarian law (IHL) does not automatically treat as unlawful, and that may in some circumstances be required by a party’s obligation to take precautions against the misuse of medical facilities. Some of this conduct is problematic, but labeling all of it “attack,” without further qualification, imports a legal conclusion the underlying facts don’t establish.

We also found, using conflict-onset data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, that 39% of logged SSA events in the occupied Palestinian territory occurred during periods that would not meet standard thresholds for active armed conflict, a precondition for the legal category of “attack” to apply at all. This suggests the SSA is, at least in part, capturing lower-level friction and violence. Such conduct is distinct from attacks governed by IHL.
articles.lede: Recent report concludes that WHO attack data cannot support the legal and comparative claims routinely built on top of it.

articles.title: 25ème session de l’Assemblée des États Parties au Statut de Rome de la Cour pénale internationale, du 30 novembre au 7 décembre 2026 (AEP25)
25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la Corte Penal Internacional
25th session of the ICC Assembly of States Parties, 30 November
25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma de la Corte Penal Internacional, del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026 (AEP25)
articles.description: Share this page Twitter Twitter Twitter Mail EN
paragraphs: Del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma se reunirán en La Haya con motivo de la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes de la Corte Penal Internacional (AEP25).

La Asamblea es el órgano de supervisión y legislativo de la Corte. Reunidos en sesión plenaria una vez al año, los Estados Partes adoptan decisiones fundamentales para el funcionamiento eficaz de la Corte y del sistema del Estatuto de Roma en su conjunto.

La AEP25 se celebra en un momento crítico para la justicia internacional. Ante la intensificación de los ataques contra la CPI, sus funcionarios, las organizaciones de la sociedad civil y otras personas y entidades que apoyan su mandato, la Asamblea brinda a los Estados Partes una oportunidad esencial para demostrar, mediante medidas concretas, su compromiso con una Corte independiente y eficaz y para proteger la integridad del sistema del Estatuto de Roma.

La sociedad civil estará presente durante toda la sesión para seguir los debates, dialogar con los Estados Partes y los funcionarios de la Corte y abogar por una CPI justa, eficaz e independiente, procurando al mismo tiempo que las perspectivas de las víctimas, las personas supervivientes y quienes defienden los derechos humanos sigan ocupando un lugar central en las deliberaciones sobre justicia y rendición de cuentas.

En su vigésima quinta sesión, la Asamblea de los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma (AEP) elegirá a seis jueces/juezas para cubrir un tercio de los 18 puestos de magistrado de la Corte Penal Internacional, conforme al ciclo electoral trienal ordinario. Cada uno/a de los/as seis jueces/juezaselegidos ejercerá un mandato de nueve años, de 2027 a 2036.

Las elecciones judiciales figuran entre las funciones de gobernanza más importantes de la Asamblea. La calidad, independencia y diversidad de los magistrados de la Corte inciden directamente en la credibilidad de la CPI, el desarrollo de su jurisprudencia y su desempeño operativo. El Estatuto de Roma establece un marco jurídico detallado destinado a garantizar que los magistrados sean seleccionados en función de sus méritos, integridad y representatividad, mientras que las resoluciones posteriores de la Asamblea han reforzado progresivamente las salvaguardias de transparencia y diligencia debida.

En vísperas de la AEP25, organizaciones de la sociedad civil y personas defensoras de los derechos humanos de todas las regiones comparten sus prioridades y recomendaciones para fortalecer la justicia a través de la CPI y del sistema del Estatuto de Roma.

Estas contribuciones son mucho más que declaraciones: reflejan las realidades vividas por quienes se encuentran en primera línea de los esfuerzos de rendición de cuentas. A lo largo de la AEP25, #NGOVoices seguirá dando visibilidad a estas perspectivas, para que las decisiones adoptadas en La Haya reflejen las necesidades y los conocimientos de quienes trabajan por la justicia en todo el mundo.
En los márgenes de la AEP25, la sociedad civil, los Estados, la Corte y otros actores organizan numerosos eventos paralelos.
articles.lede: Del 30 de noviembre al 7 de diciembre de 2026, los Estados Partes en el Estatuto de Roma se reunirán en La Haya con motivo de la 25.ª sesión de la Asamblea de los Estados Partes de la Corte Penal Internacional (AEP25).
