articles.title: Egypt: Fact-checking site’s entire newsroom jailed as assault on press freedom widens
articles.description: Six journalists who make up the entire newsroom of the Egyptian fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) said on Tuesday, warning of proliferating assaults on press freedom by the Government.
paragraphs: “ We are witnessing widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists ,” the human rights chief’s spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan told journalists in Geneva.
“ These alarming developments must end immediately, and journalists must be able to carry out their essential work free from intimidation and reprisals.”

The detained reporters are Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel. According to their lawyers, they were tortured and otherwise ill-treated and forced to record fabricated confessions.
Lina Attalah, chief editor of the independent online news outlet Mada Masr, also faces continuing judicial harassment linked to her journalistic work, the OHCHR spokesperson said.
Last month, an Egyptian court convicted her of operating an unlicensed website. She was detained, then released after paying a fine, and the court ordered the website closed.
This week, she faces another hearing in a separate case dating back to 2024 – raising fresh concerns over legal due process and the right to a fair trial, including obstacles to appeal.
OHCHR called on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information.

The authorities must release all the Matsadash reporters and drop charges arising from their legitimate journalistic work, the UN rights office said. Until then, they must have confidential access to lawyers, contact with their families, necessary healthcare and medication, and humane conditions of detention.
“ All allegations of torture, ill-treatment or forced confessions must be promptly investigated, and those responsible held to account ,” Mr. Al-Kheetan said.

articles.title: Sudan war: First ‘suicide’ drone attacks, now long-range strikes are the norm
articles.description: Drones and drought are “closing in” on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said on Tuesday, describing unprecedented attacks on the country’s infrastructure including by drones travelling up to 1,500 kilometres before hitting their target.
paragraphs: “It is an assault unlike anything Sudan has seen before. In the last week of October, not a single day passed without a drone strike on a power station in Sudan. Up to 15 were hit in the month of October,” said agency spokesperson James Elder.

“This year in Sudan, two in three child casualties were killed by armed drones. They are bringing war to places that were once safe. People in Sudan talk about three things: they talk about safety, education and water. Drones are taking all three .”
The UNICEF alert comes amid ongoing fighting between former allies turned military rivals the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

Well over 15 million people urgently require shelter across the country but drone strikes on civilians, markets and key public infrastructure continue to hinder aid efforts and increase the suffering of non-combatants.
“Several years ago, there was a use of suicide drones, which was terrifying to see that in Sudan,” Mr. Elder explained.

Highlighting the use of increasingly accurate long-range drones in the last 12 months, including some travelling 1,500 kilometres, he explained that it was impossible for humanitarian agencies like UNICEF to ascertain who was behind “at least 15 strikes” on Sudanese power stations in October. “One would struggle to think if it was in the interest of the SAF, of Government, to do that,” he added.

Straight off the plane from Sudan, Mr. Elder told journalists in Geneva about one of the many young war victims he had met from El Obeid, where UN Human Rights Council investigators say that civilians live in constant fear of drone attack.

“Buri is a teenager. An explosive took both his hands. He lives in a tent. He told me, ‘I must accept this,’” Mr. Elder explained. “ He spends the mornings learning online and the afternoons picking grass for animals with stumps for hands. His friends help him, that’s Sudan. It’s relentless. It’s crushing .”

Like Ukraine, Sudan’s energy sector is being struck repeatedly, but unlike in Ukraine, Sudanese targets are not repaired, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed: “When a power station is struck, water pumps stop, water treatment stops. Families are forced into expensive and unsafe alternatives.”
articles.lede: Drones and drought are “closing in” on Sudan, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said on Tuesday, describing unprecedented attacks on the country’s infrastructure including by drones travelling up to 1,500 kilometres…

articles.title: The legal battle over a torture centre in Kupiansk
articles.description: In northern Ukraine, a trial concerning the Russian “torture centre” in Kupiansk is unprecedented, involving dozens of victims and 18 defendants, according to the regional prosecutor’s office. But the case is struggling to make headway.
paragraphs: “I lost 18 kilos in there, and came out with grey hair,” says Larisa Fesenko, 63-year-old head and English teacher at Lisnistenkiv Secondary School in Lista Stinka, which is in the Kupiansk region of north-east Ukraine. During the Russian occupation of 2022, she spent nearly 45 days in the cells of the Kupiansk police station. According to the Ukrainian police and public prosecutor’s office, this was where one of the largest Russian torture centres in the Kharkiv region was located.

Fesenko is one of 87 victims in the Koupiansk torture centre case. Arrested on July 26, 2022, she was put in a cramped cell, where 10 to 20 other detainees were crammed onto a concrete floor covered with linoleum. “In July, the Russians abducted me straight from my home. They put a bag over my head, handcuffed me, and then took me to the torture centre,” she recounts. “I remember that day, July 26, and I will never forget it.”

The reason for her arrest? During a search of her home, the Russians found Ukrainian symbols, including a national flag that this head teacher had brought back from her school. Whilst she was striving to preserve the school’s heritage and maintain team cohesion, some of her colleagues chose to collaborate with the aggressor, according to her own account. “I was told that I would not be released under any circumstances, because I had arrived there with symbols. I was one of the political prisoners,” Fesenko continues.

The teacher says she did not betray her convictions, maintaining a pro-Ukrainian stance both at the time of her arrest and during interrogations. And she considers herself lucky: unlike others, she was subjected to neither physical violence nor electric shocks during her two interrogations, only sometimes threatened with sending her “to Belgorod” (a Russian city across the border to the north of Kharkiv), or putting her “among the deserters”. “The air in the cell was stifling. No light filtered through the windows, and we weren’t taken out into the open air,” she recalls. “We were barely fed – just noodles twice a day.”

“My place was on the floor, between two bunk beds. The toilet was in the same room,” says Fesenko. “Two people were on the bunk beds, but everyone else was on the floor – some under the beds, others near the toilet. Industrial water ran from the tap. We used it to wash and to drink.”

According to the prosecutor’s office, the arrests were unfounded and the guards forced prisoners to sing the Russian national anthem, punched and kicked them, and subjected them to electric shocks. “After the electric shocks, I had an operation on my hands. But I still haven’t regained full sensation. My hands haven’t fully regained their function,” says one of the victims quoted by the Kharkiv regional prosecutor’s office.

“At night, we could constantly hear footsteps in the corridor. They were taking people away. We sat there and could hear someone being tortured,” recalls the teacher. “The cells were open, and we could hear everything. A young man was beaten until he lost his voice, until he fell completely silent. Can you imagine? And it was like that every night.”
articles.lede: In northern Ukraine, a trial concerning the Russian “torture centre” in Kupiansk is unprecedented, involving dozens of victims and 18 defendants, according to the regional prosecutor’s office. But the case is struggling to make headway.

articles.title: Eyes in the sky, weapons in hand: FPV drones and the challenges for IHL and the protection of civilians
articles.description: FPV drones, IHL compliance and the growing challenges of protecting civilians in armed conflict.
paragraphs: Drones have become a defining feature of contemporary armed conflicts. Their use has surged dramatically in recent years, originally with the proliferation of inexpensive, commercially available systems, and increasingly with militaries also manufacturing drones at scale. Among these, first-person view (FPV) drones – small, agile aircraft controlled by an operator with a live video stream directly from the drone’s camera – have emerged as a particularly versatile tool. Small, cheap, and easy to assemble and operate, FPV drones have reportedly been used by both state and non-state armed actors in conflicts across all regions of the world, including in Latin America, Gaza, Syria, Iran and elsewhere in West Asia, the Sahel (e.g. Mali ), Sudan, Ukraine, Thailand and Cambodia, and Myanmar.

In this post, ICRC Advisers Georgia Hinds, Mauro Vignati and Eirini Giorgou examine how FPV drones are reshaping the conduct of hostilities, with implications for civilians in armed conflict and for compliance with international humanitarian law (IHL). They go on to suggest practical measures that parties to armed conflict should take to address these risks and ensure respect for IHL.

The term “first-person view” has its roots in video games of the 1970s, in which the player could experience the game through the eyes of a character. Originally developed for civilian use, particularly hobby flying and drone racing, FPV drones are characterized by a front-facing camera transmitting live footage to the operator, enabling immersive control beyond line of sight. This relatively simple innovation has made FPV drones highly adaptable for military use. Technological improvements – enhanced maneuverability, increased payload capacity, extended range or flight time, and the integration of thermal cameras – have further expanded their operational utility.

Recent developments also point toward increasing autonomy. Some FPV drones can continue flying toward a pre-designated target even when communication with the operator is disrupted. While autonomy in navigation on its own does not make an FPV drone an autonomous weapon system, it illustrates a broader trend toward reduced human involvement in certain functions.
These drones are now used for both surveillance and attack, often in combination with other systems, in addition to less traditional tasks such as the acceptance of surrender by adversaries. [1]

FPV drones are increasingly used to carry out attacks in armed conflict. They are typically armed with explosive payloads which are then dropped onto targets or detonate when the drone crashes into a target. They can be used individually or in coordinated swarms to target personnel or equipment. Whilst FPV drones are still predominantly “multirotor” configurations, fixed-wing models are increasingly being used to extend range, speed and payload capacity, with reported examples of operational range now reaching 30 kilometers.

Some FPV drones may “loiter” for periods of time. They can be used in ambush-style operations, kept concealed until a target appears and the operator detonates the munition. Others are reported to be configured to detonate upon movement or tampering. It is extremely difficult to verify these claims and technical capabilities. But such “victim-activated” systems may qualify as mines or booby-traps, governed by the relevant treaty and customary IHL rules, or as autonomous weapon systems if they can select and engage a target based on its movement without further human intervention, in which case the ICRC’s recommendations on autonomous weapons are especially relevant.
articles.lede: FPV drones, IHL compliance and the growing challenges of protecting civilians in armed conflict.

articles.title: Generating the New World: A Critical Perspective on EJIL’s Policy on Gen AI Use
articles.description: Introduction EJIL’s first Policy on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) was introduced in July 2026, with an editorial comment by Sarah Nouwen and Michael Waibel. Such Gen AI policie…
paragraphs: EJIL’s first Policy on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) was introduced in July 2026, with an editorial comment by Sarah Nouwen and Michael Waibel. Such Gen AI policies have been adopted by major international law journals, such as AJIL, ICLQ, and LJIL under CUP’s policy, and JICJ, JCSL, and JIDS under OUP’s policy. The general trend is the obligation to disclose Gen AI use beyond minimal uses such as language checking, authors’ responsibility for manuscripts involving AI, and the denial of authorship to AI. The EJIL policy is apparently restrictive in its prohibition of certain ways of Gen AI use by introducing its human-AI outweighing approach (para. 3). One might question whether the policy really fits the reality of widespread Gen AI use, as already acknowledged by the policy’s statement that Gen AI ‘is increasingly being used in academic research and writing’ (para. 1).

Throughout human history, revolutionary technological developments have redefined what counts as necessary competencies for life and work, including scholarly work. Overly rigid policies on Gen AI use that pose a high or unclear hurdle for such use, in combination with the disclosure obligation and the possibility of severe sanctions, could have significant repercussions for other academic societies and journals, especially when adopted by prominent journals such as EJIL. This would risk hampering the necessary transformation of scholarly work.

Against this background, I venture to submit a fundamental critique of EJIL’s Gen AI policy. While Niccolò Ridi has already posted an excellent argument primarily about the enforcement aspect of the policy on this blog, my argument questions the underlying logic and premises of the policy, drawing on such concepts as dynamic interplay, absolute authorial accountability, and the transparency dilemma.

Let me clarify the structure of the policy. Paragraph 1 provides the statement of the principle that ‘while Gen AI may complement, it should not replace, human intelligence in scholarly production’, and paragraph 3(a) sets out two requirements: ‘the submission contains a significant intellectual contribution’ and ‘the intellectual contribution of the named author(s) clearly outweighs the contribution of Gen AI’. When Gen AI’s contribution, ‘if made by a human’, would warrant the status of a co-author, the outweighing test is not met (para. 3(a)(ii)). Those formulations are to be interpreted ‘by reference to legal-academic best practice on authorship and responsibility’ (para. 3(b)), based on an ‘analogy’, as explained by the editorial comment. There are two points to be made about this structure. First, it is doubtful that existing practice is clear enough to allow an objective assessment of whether a research assistant’s contribution deserves co-authorship or only acknowledgement, even in traditional settings involving only humans. The mere collection of relevant literature requires substantive, in some cases, normative judgements on what constitutes relevance in particular contexts. For me, Joseph Weiler’s emphasis on ab initio discussion with research assistants about co-authorship suggests the inherent difficulties, at least in legal scholarship, of leaving this to the determination of a third party, who was not involved in that research process.
articles.lede: EJIL’s first Policy on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) was introduced in July 2026, with an editorial comment by Sarah Nouwen and Michael Waibel.

articles.title: How the UN Bought Time for the World to Understand Autonomous Weapons
articles.description: UN bought essential time for States and armed forces to reveal the principles and practices of AI-enabled LAWS.
paragraphs: As the UN Group of Governmental Experts (GGE) concludes its decade-long mandate on lethal autonomous weapon systems (LAWS), its final report does little more than reiterate existing International Humanitarian Law (IHL). However, its value should not be judged as a failed legal endeavour, but as a protracted holding pattern that absorbed public moral panic and protected against premature vetoes or restrictions. In delaying top-down regulation, it bought essential time for States and armed forces to reveal the principles and practices of AI-enabled LAWS. This process provided opponents and proponents with technical ground truth rather than sci-fi hype.

The humanitarian risks from “Killer Robots” digitally dehumanising combatants and killing civilians dominated the public conscience in the early 2010s. The combination of uncrewed aircraft and emerging AI presented a fantastical science fiction threat that urgently needed to be controlled or banned. The GGE was established in 2017 to respond to concerns that existing controls were insufficient for novel LAWS.

As a mechanism to inform global regulation, the GGE’s initial progress appeared painfully slow, with huge effort expended just trying to define the problems it was meant to solve. In 2019, it agreed on eleven “ guiding principles” to shape the group’s work. In 2023 the UN Secretary General called on world leaders to launch negotiations of a new legally binding instrument, with the GGE mandated to formulate the “set of elements” to guide this future work. As the 2026 Report concludes this task of international consensus-building and prepares the ground for even more negotiations, we must ask whether the GGE’s involvement was necessary or desirable?

The panic surrounding LAWS made political outsourcing inevitable. Orben’s The Sisyphean Cycle of Technology Panics highlights political distancing as an established and typical response to threats from new technology. The cycle’s first stage, “panic creation,” is characterised by actors highlighting the risks of new technology in broad, and often misleading, terms. For LAWS, this included the Stop Killer Robots Campaigners’ Kit, which helped create widespread fear of autonomous killing.

This moral panic then feeds the second stage, “political outsourcing,” whereby politicians push the debate to external contestation. LAWS contestation was outsourced to the GGE and its multinational, NGO and scientific membership.

Despite the GGE’s protracted contestation, its eventual consensus has produced very little that is different from the prohibitions and restrictions already in place for other weapons. The overwhelming majority of the report can therefore be seen as standard weapons controls.

In the report, IHL remains the central principle for LAWS use, and there are a few LAWS-specific elements to guide their design. For example, software must be locked down and understood, operational effects must be limitable, and a human must be responsible and accountable for each use. The requirement that “those responsible for the use of LAWS can limit their effects” is already a fundamental requirement of command and control.
articles.lede: UN bought essential time for States and armed forces to reveal the principles and practices of AI-enabled LAWS.

articles.title: Beyond the broken glass: The human cost of the 1938 November Pogrom
articles.description: On his way to school in Vienna on the morning of 10 November 1938, eight-year-old Arthur Schneier watched his synagogue burn while firefighters and police officers stood by “rejoicing”.
paragraphs: More than 87 years later, Rabbi Schneier told a UN panel in New York that the memory has never left him.

It shaped a lifelong conviction, he said in a video recording: an attack on a community’s house of worship strikes at the very heart of its faith. His message was one of mutual respect and acceptance, and a call for everyone to learn from the past.

The panel was held this week ahead of the 88th anniversary of the Kristallnacht pogrom, when years of State-sponsored antisemitism erupted into orchestrated violence against Jewish communities across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland.
Speakers set out to look past the familiar images of shattered shop windows to the fear, grief and loss lived by Jewish children, parents and neighbours.
On the night of 9–10 November 1938, synagogues were set alight, Jewish homes and businesses were ransacked and some 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.

It marked a turning point: Nazi persecution of Jews moved from discrimination and exclusion to open violence on the streets. Many tried to flee, only to find that other countries would not take them in.

The Nazis called it Kristallnacht – “crystal night”, or the night of broken glass. The name came from the shards that littered the streets, but it was a euphemism that played down the violence done to people.
The photographs remain: Jewish men forced to march through their towns with their heads uncovered; neighbours looking on; synagogues desecrated; homes and businesses ransacked.
But what do these images really tell us about the people who lived through the pogrom? And what do they leave out?
articles.lede: On his way to school in Vienna on the morning of 10 November 1938, eight-year-old Arthur Schneier watched his synagogue burn while firefighters and police officers stood by “rejoicing”.

articles.title: GC IV Commentary Series – Article 47 of the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949: A Possible Blind Spot
articles.description: The interpretation of Article 47 of GC IV raises a general legal issue: the proper balance between rigidity and flexibility.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Although the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) updated Commentary offers thorough treatment, the aim of this post is to cast additional light on two sides of the coin that is Article 47 of the 1949 Fourth Geneva Convention (GC IV). First, we will explore the true scope and content of the provision to give it proper interpretation.

Second, we will consider whether there are some situations for which the regulation of Article 47 is not fully adapted, namely, situations which lead to a normative blind spot. This may be the case especially in prolonged occupations, where agreements must to some extent adapt the situation to new realities. The aim of these agreements must not be to deprive civilians of their rights, although exactly that may incidentally occur to some extent. Would then Article 47 entail a responsibility of the parties to the agreement, or even cause it to become void? This question is explored here to supplement the coverage offered by the updated Commentary.

Protected persons who are in occupied territory shall not be deprived, in any case or in any manner whatsoever, of the benefits of the present Convention by any change introduced, as the result of the occupation of a territory, into the institutions or government of the said territory, nor by any agreement concluded between the authorities of the occupied territories and the Occupying Power, nor by any annexation by the latter of the whole or part of the occupied territory.

The article aims to maintain the legal effectiveness of the rights and especially the obligations incumbent upon an occupying power (i.e. the rights of the civilians in occupied territory). An occupant may well be tempted by an all-too-easy pretext to evade its duties as occupier if it could, for example, annex the territory and pretend that, being now on its own national territory, it would not owe obligations under the law of occupation. The aim of Article 47 is thus to close the way to such circumventing action and to forestall a glaring and threatening gap in the law of occupation.
In this regard, Article 47 is fundamental. In the words of the recent updated ICRC GC IV Commentary,

Its placement underscores the importance of this rule, establishing as it does the inviolability of the benefits guaranteed by the Convention to protected persons in occupied territory and ensuring that they are not deprived of those benefits in any way. It is a key safeguard in relation to all the other provisions in the Convention that are applicable during occupation (para. 3097).

Despite its fundamental character, it must be recalled that Article 47 is a mere jus in bello provision without any jus ad bellum component. In this sense, Article 47 does not prohibit annexation of territory. The prohibition of annexation is contained in the jus ad bellum and is attached to Article 2(4) of the UN Charter. Instead, the point of Article 47 is merely to state that even if the described action takes place (e.g. an annexation occurs) protected persons cannot be stripped of their rights and the occupying power concomitantly does not free itself of its corresponding obligations.
articles.lede: The interpretation of Article 47 of GC IV raises a general legal issue: the proper balance between rigidity and flexibility.

articles.title: Afghanistan faces deepening humanitarian crisis amid sweeping rights restrictions
articles.description: Afghanistan stands at a “difficult crossroad” more than five years after the Taliban returned to power, a senior UN official said on Friday. Relative stability and security are being undercut by a fragile economy, sweeping curbs on rights and acute humanitarian need.
paragraphs: Bruno Lemarquis is the Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Afghanistan. He is also the UN’s Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in the country.
Women and girls continue to suffer from “severe and sweeping” restrictions on their freedoms, being deprived of many spaces to learn, work and participate in public life, Mr. Lemarquis stressed.
In particular, the restriction of girls’ access to education represents “one of the world’s most sensitive…education challenges,” he said.
Since 2021, over 2.6 million girls have been denied secondary education, and female university enrollment currently stands at zero.
But higher education overall is in crisis: due to the country’s economic frailty, some families are also holding back from sending their boys to school.

When asked by a journalist how the Taliban justify their restrictions on women and girls, Mr. Lemarquis said their explanations are a mix of religious extremism and deep historical practices of control and discrimination.
Since September 2025, Afghan women staffers have also been banned from entering United Nations premises across the country, and the ban has not been lifted.
The “massive” return of 6.7 million nationals to Afghanistan since 2020 is also placing additional strain on its already stretched services.
Many were forcibly expelled from the neighbouring countries that were hosting them, with a large portion coming from Pakistan and Iran.
articles.lede: Afghanistan stands at a “difficult crossroad” more than five years after the Taliban returned to power, a senior UN official said on Friday.

articles.title: Syria: a map of trials since the fall of Assad
articles.description: Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime on December 8, 2024, the Syrian judiciary has brought charges against several dozen people accused of serious crimes committed under the former regime and since the start of the transition.
paragraphs: These promises of justice come as a response to strong demands from the Syrian people and the international community. Hearings have been held in Damascus and Aleppo, some of which have received extensive media coverage. Public prosecutors’ offices dedicated to transitional justice cases are being established in Homs and Latakia. Proceedings are not all held in the same way: some are public, others take place behind closed doors, and several defendants are being tried in absentia. Here we list the criminal proceedings that are currently known, almost two years after Assad’s fall.

Below, Justice Info presents a map accompanied by a summary of the figures and visual data. All of this data (finalised in early November 2026) is set out in more detail in an article further down the page.

On November 18, 2025, the trial began concerning violence that struck the Syrian coast in March 2025, resulting in more than 1,400 deaths among Alawite civilians. This trial in Aleppo (north-west Syria) represents a response by the current government to the massacres. Seven militiamen loyal to the former regime and seven members of the new security forces were tried over the course of 16 hearings, held both in public and in camera. On September 17 and October 15, 2026, the military court handed down 11 convictions and 2 acquittals.

In 2026, the Syrian capital has seen several trials organised on crimes attributed to former officials and leading figures of the Assad regime, including Bashar al-Assad himself. The majority are being heard by the Fourth Criminal Chamber of the Damascus Courthouse.

• On April 26, 2026, the Fourth Criminal Chamber in Damascus opened its first major trial, with Atef Najib, former head of political security in Deraa (southern Syria), Bashar al-Assad and seven other officials being tried in absentia. They include the former president’s brother Maher Hafez al-Assad and former defence minister Fahd Jassem al-Freij. Najib, who was arrested on April 7, 2026, appeared at nine hearings. The court heard dozens of witnesses with regard to the arrest and alleged torture of children, shooting of demonstrators, and events that took place at the al-Omari Mosque. On August 11, 2026, the court delivered its 396-page judgement. “The document will be published at a later date on the Ministry of Justice’s official website, once the names of protected witnesses have been redacted,” the official Syrian news agency Sana stated in a press release. The court found Najib guilty of murder and ordering the shooting of demonstrators. It described the acts as crimes against humanity and sentenced him to death. On the same day, the court handed down death sentences in absentia against Bashar al-Assad and seven other senior officials.
In a statement to Sana, Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan, president of the Fourth Criminal Chamber, announced that the judgments handed down in absentia would be forwarded to Interpol.

• On June 14, 2026, the trial of Abdel Nasser al-Burraqi began before the Fourth Criminal Chamber at the Damascus Courthouse. Described as an informant for the former regime, he was charged with enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, complicity in premeditated murder, torture resulting in death, robbery with violence and false accusation. On August 27, 2026, he was found guilty of all these crimes. In classifying them as war crimes and crimes against humanity, the court drew on international law. It applied Syrian law in determining the sentence. Al-Burraqi was sentenced to death, with seizure of all his assets.

GC IV Commentary Series
articles.description: 2025 Commentary’s discussion of Common Article 2(2) - 2(3) has done a good job of clarifying these provisions, but more could have been done.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

Most discussion concerning Article 2 common (CA 2) to the four 1949 Geneva Conventions involves the first paragraph of the article, the application trigger for the law of armed conflict (LOAC) to “armed conflict which may arise between two or more of the High Contracting Parties,” or international armed conflict (IAC), as it has come to be known. However, the text of CA 2 also includes two additional, though much less frequently discussed paragraphs: a second paragraph addressing occupation; and a third paragraph discussing the application of LOAC to armed conflicts between States when not all belligerents are parties to the Conventions.
[(2)] The Convention shall also apply to all cases of partial or total occupation of the territory of a High Contracting Party, even if the said occupation meets with no armed resistance.

[(3)] Although one of the Powers in conflict may not be a party to the present Convention, the Powers who are parties thereto shall remain bound by it in their mutual relations. They shall furthermore be bound by the Convention in relation to the said Power, if the latter accepts and applies the provisions thereof.

A 2025 Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention (the Commentary ), by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), on paragraphs 2(2) and 2(3) is more extensive than a preceding 1958 Commentary (1956 in French) and is a very helpful addition to the corpus of discussion of these two paragraphs. However, the updated Commentary also raises three points worth closer examination: 1) belligerent occupation, including missed opportunities to clarify contemporary issues; 2) the requirement of an explicit statement for non-parties to not be bound by the Conventions; and 3) the potential application of the Conventions to “International Organizations” but not to non-States. This post addresses each of these three points in detail below.

Common Article 2 says very little about occupation, though the Fourth Geneva Convention (GC IV) offers quite a bit of detail in subsequent provisions with respect to laws that apply during occupation. It is important to note that CA 2(2) is not intended to refer to occupation generally, but only applies to the narrow situation of an unopposed occupation. As the 1958 Commentary makes clear,

The sense in which the paragraph under consideration should be understood is thus quite clear. It does not refer to cases in which territory is occupied during hostilities; in such cases the Convention will have been in force since the outbreak of hostilities or since the time war was declared. The paragraph only refers to cases where the occupation has taken place without a declaration of war and without hostilities, and makes provision for the entry into force of the Convention in those particular circumstances (p. 21).
articles.lede: 2025 Commentary’s discussion of Common Article 2(2) - 2(3) has done a good job of clarifying these provisions, but more could have been done.

articles.title: The Swedish Commission closes the Nordic Sami reconciliation initiatives
articles.description: On September 30, 2026, Sweden has joined its Nordic neighbours in delivering a Sami Truth Commission report. Following five years of work and 270 interviews, its chair emphasised the urgent need for an official apology.
paragraphs: On September 30, 2026, the Truth Commission for the Sami People handed over its final report at its ceremonial closing in Staare/Östersund, Sweden. This was the last of the Nordic truth commissions for the Indigenous Sami people to conclude its work, following the Norwegian report delivered in 2023 and the Finnish report presented in 2025.

The ceremony was carried out in Swedish and some of the five different varieties of the Sami language, via an app’ for live interpretation. Several hundreds of people attended in person in the aula of the Staare/Östersund campus of the University of Mid-Sweden. Throughout the three hours of the ceremony, between 300 and 500 people watched the live broadcasting [still available online ]. The comment section proved a lively place for participants to express their own stories as well as support to others, either in Swedish, in Sami, or in emoji. Hearts and clapping hands flooded the comment section with each moving speech, flanked by messages expressing gratitude and personal experiences underscoring for example the need for language revitalization. It also came to function as a forum for translation questions, with attendees helping each other out. With the closing of the live stream, participants expressed hope and desire for implementation of the recommendations.

All the Nordic truth commissions have been influenced by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, which delivered its report in 2015. In his welcome speech at the handover ceremony, Jerker Bexelius, leader of the Gaaltije museum in Staare/Östersund, pointed out that it coincided with Canada’s national day for truth and reconciliation.

The commission, mandated by the Swedish government in 2021, began its work in June 2022, and has had three different chairs. At the ceremony, Lena Nyberg, who took over in April 2025, urged for an independent mechanism to monitor implementation of the truth commission’s calls to action and proposals. Furthermore, she called for increased autonomy of the Swedish Sami Parliament, a range of initiatives to increase the general public’s knowledge about Sami culture, history and rights, and measures to combat racism and discrimination against Sami. Nyberg also emphasised the need for an official apology — similar to the one already given by the Norwegian Parliament — and the urgent need for a special apology to elderly Sami who had been placed in so-called nomad schools or other boarding school facilities as children.

Different commissioners presented further findings and calls to action, highlighting the loss of language and culture, acts of resistance, the consequences of state and majority-population ignorance, and the Sami relationship to land use and ownership. These presentations were interspersed with readings of testimonies based on the personal narratives collected by the commission; circa 270 interviews as well as 40 written narratives and some focus group interviews with children and youth. Excerpts from these stories are presented in a separate part of the final report which was handed out to members of the audience.
articles.lede: On September 30, 2026, Sweden has joined its Nordic neighbours in delivering a Sami Truth Commission report. Following five years of work and 270 interviews, its chair emphasised the urgent need for an official apology.

articles.title: Cases against Italy before European Court of Human Rights could clarify States’ duty to cooperate with international justice amid mounting threats to the ICC
articles.description: Italy's ICC cooperation is challenged before the European Court of Human Rights as NGOs intervene in cases concerning the release of a Libya war crimes suspect.
paragraphs: 2 November 2026 – REDRESS, Route Justice, TRIAL International, and the International Federation for Human Rights ( FIDH) have submitted third-party interventions to the European Court of Human Rights in two cases challenging Italy’s failure to surrender Osama Elmasry Njeem to the International Criminal Court (ICC). While REDRESS, Route Justice, and TRIAL international argue that States’ human rights obligations generally require them to cooperate with the ICC to ensure accountability for torture and other international crimes, FIDH’s intervention addresses the admissibility of the applications

The cases ( Y v. Italy and Z v. Italy) concern Osama Elmasry Njeem, who was wanted by the ICC for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Libya. He was arrested in Italy in January 2025, released two days later and returned to Libya on a State flight.

These cases raise a question with implications far beyond Italy: when surrendering a suspect to an international court is essential to securing accountability, can a State’s failure to cooperate breach its human rights obligations under the European Convention on Human Rights?
The victims in the case allege that Italy’s conduct breached its obligations under the rights to life and freedom from torture.

REDRESS, Route Justice, and TRIAL International argue that a suspect’s presence on a State’s territory, a request for arrest and surrender from a competent international court, international obligations to investigate the alleged crimes, and the absence of a realistic alternative avenue for accountability can together establish the jurisdictional link needed to engage the State’s procedural obligations under Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention (the right to life and the prohibition of torture). Once those obligations are engaged, they may require meaningful cooperation with the international court where this is reasonably necessary to secure effective accountability.

The intervention asks the European Court to recognise that, where international proceedings offer the only realistic prospect of accountability, States must use the powers reasonably available to them diligently, effectively, and in good faith. Their conduct must be assessed against their wider international obligations, including obligations under the Rome Statute and the peremptory prohibitions of torture and crimes against humanity.

FIDH has filed a separate third-party intervention in the same cases. It argues that the Assembly of States Parties’ non-cooperation procedure following an ICC finding does not bar individual applications under the European Convention. FIDH maintains that the procedures concern different parties and complaints, and that the Assembly’s procedure is not comparable to an international investigation or settlement, given its distinct features and potential effects, which differ from those of individual applications seeking redress for violations of Convention rights.

The cases come at a critical moment for the ICC, which faces sanctions and other measures aimed at obstructing its work and intimidating those who work for or cooperate with it. These threats make effective State cooperation all the more important to safeguarding access to international justice.

The VRWG is a network of 181 civil society organisations working to uphold the rights and interests of victims in International Criminal Court (ICC) proceedings. Co-led by the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), REDRESS and the Coalition for the ICC, the VRWG was reconvened in 2024 to renew its engagement on victims’ rights at the ICC, including contributing to the Court’s review of its 2012 Victims’ Strategy.

articles.title: Breaking the silence in Mexico’s barracks
articles.description: In Mexico’s armed forces, an order from a superior is meant to be obeyed without question. For many women in uniform, investigative journalist Zorayda Gallegos found, that can include an order to step into an officer’s bedroom.
paragraphs: “If an officer says, ‘Come into my bedroom,’ she must go in, otherwise she would be disobeying an order from her superior,” she told UN News.

Her investigation into sexual violence inside the military has won her the 2026 Breach/Valdez Award for Journalism and Human Rights. It has also made her a target, in one of the most dangerous countries in the world to be a reporter.
Her story, told ahead of the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes Against Journalists on Monday, shows both why a free press matters and how much it can cost.
Her report, Sexual violence in the barracks: an X-ray of impunity, tracked more than 520 women who reported sexual offences over a 12-year period.
Only three per cent of those cases ended in a conviction. The other 97 per cent led to no effective sanctions.
This is not an isolated problem, Ms. Gallegos says, but a structural one. It reaches beyond the barracks into military schools and hospitals.
She also documented how high-ranking officials cover up abuse, and how gender inequality and institutional obstacles discourage victims from filing complaints at all.

For Ms. Gallegos, part of the problem starts with military training itself, which she describes as “a very hierarchical, top-down system where women are always taught to follow orders from their superiors”.

Deep-rooted sexism makes things worse, she maintains, shaping who gets which jobs and who gets promoted. Female soldiers are often assigned tasks associated with “caregiving and nursing, even though they are qualified for higher-ranking positions,” she explains.

Contemporary accomplices? Considering the potential liability of AI targeting system providers under the Rome Statute
articles.description: Could AI targeting system providers face criminal liability for war crimes? Explore how the Rome Statute addresses corporate complicity in international crimes.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled targeting systems are increasingly being used in armed conflicts to process data and provide lists of military objectives. This raises a difficult question that has received little attention: Could the senior executives of the technology companies that provide these systems face criminal liability under international law when their systems contribute to serious violations of international humanitarian law?

In this post, part of our Emerging Voices series, Rosa Villar Orero, PhD candidate at the University of Aberdeen, argues that Article 25(3)(d)(ii) of the Rome Statute, as operationalized through the Katanga test, offers a potential doctrinal avenue for establishing the criminal liability of AI targeting system providers whose contribution is made with knowledge of a group’s intention to commit such crimes.

In 1946, a British military tribunal convicted Bruno Tesch for complicity in the murder of millions of people at Auschwitz. Tesch was a businessman who ran Tesch & Stabenow, a company that supplied concentration camps with a poisonous gas called Zyklon B. Although h e never entered a camp and never issued an order to kill, merely sat in his office, processed contracts, and shipped chemicals, h e was nonetheless found liable. The reasoning was simple: Tesch had knowingly provided the means by which others committed mass atrocity. Physical proximity to the crime was not relevant; what mattered was the structural relationship between his conduct and the crime.

Nearly eighty years later, the question that emerges is: what would Tesch look like today? He would not be selling chemicals. Instead, would he be selling algorithms? As AI services are increasingly used by parties to armed conflict in the conduct of hostilities, it is time to take a fresh look at the precedent for holding companies that provide products and services to warring parties accountable for their contribution, in the case that those parties commit serious violations of international humanitarian law.

In contemporary armed conflicts, AI-enabled targeting systems are being deployed to process vast amounts of data to generate lists of military objectives. These systems dramatically increase the speed and scale of target production. They correlate data, find patterns, and recommend targets – in some reported cases, at a rate that human analysts could never match.

Behind these systems stand technology corporations. Their executives are not in the field or issuing strike orders. They are sitting in urban centers often far from the physical site of attacks, approving contracts. Yet, if these systems are deployed in the commission of war crimes at a large scale, the support those technologies provide becomes legally significant, bringing the following question:
Can the senior executives of technology companies whose AI systems contribute to the commission of war crimes be held criminally liable under the Rome Statute?

Technology corporations are primarily driven by the maximization of profits. Their AI systems are designed and sold as legitimate commercial products. Accordingly, proving that a CEO approved a contract with the purpose of facilitating a war crime is, in practice, evidentially difficult.
articles.lede: Could AI targeting system providers face criminal liability for war crimes? Explore how the Rome Statute addresses corporate complicity in international crimes.

articles.title: BELARUS: Swiss Court Convicts Former Security Officer of Enforced Disappearance
articles.description: In a historic first, a Swiss court convicts Yuri Harauski of enforced disappearance in Belarus under universal jurisdiction, overturning his 2023 acquittal.
paragraphs: (St. Gallen, Paris, Minsk, Geneva, 26 October 2026) – The Cantonal Court of St. Gallen has convicted former Special Rapid Response Unit (SOBR) member Yuri Harauski of the enforced disappearance of Anatoly Krasouski in Belarus in 1999, overturning his 2023 acquittal on appeal. The court also established his participation in the enforced disappearances of Yuri Zakharenka and Viktar Hanchar, but upheld Harauski’s acquittal for legal reasons. The court reduced Harauski’s sentence from eight to a two-year suspended prison term, considering his confession and public apology to the victims.

Following an appeal trial held on 22 September 2026, the Court found Yuri Harauski guilty of the enforced disappearance of well-known Belarusian businessman Anatoly Krasouski in 1999. The Court, however, upheld his acquittal in relation to the disappearances of Yury Zakharenka and Viktar Hanchar. The former member of the SOBR was sentenced to two years’ imprisonment, suspended.

Today’s conviction marks the first time a member of the Belarusian security apparatus has been convicted abroad for crimes committed as part of the repression under Aliaksandr Lukashenka’s regime and the first time anywhere in the world that a court ruled on crimes committed in Belarus under the principle of universal jurisdiction. The case was also the first in which the crime of enforced disappearance was examined before a Swiss court.

The conviction marks a significant step towards accountability for crimes committed under Aliaksandr Lukashenka’s regime and an important development in Switzerland and beyond. “ I feel relieved to have received the guilty verdict ”, said Valeriya Krasouskaya, daughter of Anatoly Krasousky. “ After 27 years, at least one of the numerous persons involved in the abduction and murder of my father is officially recognised guilty .”

TRIAL International, the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and Human Rights Center Viasna, which initiated the proceedings together with relatives of two of the disappeared men in 2021, welcome the conviction as an important step towards accountability.

“ For years, impunity for crimes committed under Lukashenka’s regime has looked unassailable. This verdict proves it is not — investigators, prosecutors and courts now have a precedent showing that accountability for Belarusian state crimes is achievable ”, said Philip Grant, TRIAL International’s Executive Director.

The significance of the judgement may extend beyond Harauski’s own case: by establishing criminal responsibility for acts carried out by a member of the SOBR, it could contribute to broader efforts to examine the chain of responsibility behind the enforced disappearances, including the role of those who ordered or directed the crimes.

“ The conviction of Yuri Harauski for his involvement in the enforced disappearance of Anatoly Krasouski in Belarus is, first and foremost, a victory for his family, who have finally seen justice served after many years of efforts ”, said Alexis Deswaef, FIDH President. “ We are grateful to the Swiss justice system for demonstrating that this is possible by advancing international justice based on the principles of universal jurisdiction .”
articles.lede: In a historic first, a Swiss court convicts Yuri Harauski of enforced disappearance in Belarus under universal jurisdiction, overturning his 2023 acquittal.

Yesterday’s children: now is the time to repatriate the children – and the young people who have “aged out” of childhood – in the camps and prisons of north-east Syria and Iraq
articles.description: They were children when it began. The ICRC calls for their return from Syria and Iraq, including young adults left behind.
paragraphs: Several years after the Islamic State group lost its last territory in March 2019, tens of thousands of Syrians, Iraqis, and third-country nationals from around 60 countries – including many children – remained in camps and prisons in north-east Syria and Iraq. In early 2026, almost 6,000 detainees were transferred to Iraq, among them children who were caught up in a war they did not choose. Repatriation remains the best way forward for most of the third-country nationals – but a deeply disturbing trend concerns the exclusion of young third-country nationals who “age out” of childhood from repatriation efforts.

In this post, ICRC Advisers Julia Joerin, Vanessa Murphy, and Katerina Kappos lay out why states should include young adults in repatriations as a standard practice, and call on states to reaffirm their commitment to resolving what continues to be one of the most complex and protracted child protection crises of our time.

Before the political shifts that took place in north-east Syria earlier this year, tens of thousands of Syrians, Iraqis and third-country nationals from around 60 countries were held in the region’s camps and places of detention, most of them arbitrarily, and a majority women and children. They have long been collectively perceived as affiliated with the Islamic State group, regardless of individual circumstances or their age. Over the last decade, the ICRC witnessed first-hand how these places became a microcosm of suffering and despair.

But then the situation in the camps and places of detention changed rapidly – including through the transfer of almost 6,000 detainees to Iraq. There is now a window of opportunity to act in the interests of the children and young people who have been too long forgotten.

Over recent years, several states assumed responsibility for their nationals in north-east Syria and in Iraq, bringing children home, reuniting families, and showing how this can be done humanely and safely. Around 3,400 third-country nationals (including many children) were repatriated by 58 countries of origin between 2019 and 2026.
But today, across Syria and Iraq an estimated 2,000 children of third-country nationality are still stranded, waiting to go back home with their families.

In addition, many children captured during 2017-2019 military operations have since turned 18, meaning they no longer fall under the legal definition of “child”. They are now “aged out” young adults, with little prospect to be repatriated with their families and a high risk of being left behind.

For several years, the ICRC conducted regular visits to the camps in north-east Syria, and operated a medical centre in Al-Hol camp together with the Syrian Arab Red Crescent. It was also often the only humanitarian actor able to access juvenile and adult places of detention, including “rehabilitation” centres, to monitor treatment and living conditions and to address some of the most pressing humanitarian needs. The ICRC’s visits offered detainees and people held in camps the possibility to exchange family news with their loved ones. The ICRC also notified states of the whereabouts of their nationals held in camps and places of detention, as per the wishes of the latter, who in most cases want to be repatriated to their country of origin.

articles.title: President Gatti Santana addresses United Nations General Assembly
articles.description: The President of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism), Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, today presented the Mechanism’s fourteenth annual report to the United Nations General Assembly in New York. At the outset, President Gatti Santana wished His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh every success in his role as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly, noting that his focus on peace and security, respect for international law, and commitment to multilateralism is essential in these times.
paragraphs: At the outset, President Gatti Santana wished His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh every success in his role as President of the 81st session of the General Assembly, noting that his focus on peace and security, respect for international law, and commitment to multilateralism is essential in these times.

President Gatti Santana then referred to the award of the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay noting that she had served as the first woman Judge of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and its second President and had participated in landmark rulings that advanced accountability and justice for crimes that shock the conscience. President Gatti Santana highlighted that the justice cycle that commenced with those rulings is not complete, and that the Assembly’s support now at the end of the justice cycle is as important as the support provided to start it. She emphasized, in particular, the United Nations’ ongoing obligations to guarantee the fundamental rights of those convicted, as well as the judicial protection of thousands of victims and witnesses who courageously testified. She further stressed that the archives managed by the Mechanism are the property of the United Nations and require continued management for permanent preservation.

President Gatti Santana continued by assuring the Assembly that the responsible and appropriate conclusion of the Mechanism’s justice cycle is within reach. She referred, in particular, to the comprehensive strategic plan that the Mechanism presented to the Security Council in May 2026, which, building upon recommendations of the Secretary-General and the United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services, provides a blueprint for the conclusion of all activities with clear implementation timelines. The plan specifically identifies which functions can end, which can be transferred, and those which must remain at the international level. In this regard, President Gatti Santana emphasised her unequivocal support for the Secretary-General’s recommendation that the authority over pardon, commutation of sentence and early release remain at the international level. She highlighted that retaining international jurisdiction on such matters safeguards the consistent application of the governing legal framework, legal certainty, and the involvement of judges familiar with the relevant cases, conflicts and sentencing practice.

However, as President Gatti Santana noted, the Mechanism requires a Security Council resolution to enact the radical transformation set out in the strategic plan. In the interim, the General Assembly has a critical role to play in ensuring that the United Nations’ investment in international criminal justice is not lost.

President Gatti Santana observed that the recent “hero’s funeral” that Mr. Ratko Mladić was accorded in Belgrade underscores the potential perils of faltering in this final phase of the justice cycle. She referred to the observations of a number of United Nations experts and special rapporteurs who warned that public actions that appear to honour individuals found responsible for atrocities “risk undermining decades of efforts to seek truth, end impunity and achieve justice and reparations for these crimes”, and that “[i]f such blatant genocide denial succeeds, it will roll back international criminal accountability gains against impunity that were forged in the fires of Nuremberg and Tokyo, and the International Criminal Tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda.”
articles.lede: The President of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism), Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, today presented the Mechanism’s fourteenth annual report to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

articles.title: As Sudan war spills into Central African Republic, UN warns against early peacekeeper exit
articles.description: The UN warned on Tuesday against a premature withdrawal of its peacekeepers as the war in Sudan spills over into the Central African Republic (CAR).
paragraphs: CAR continues to face a resurgence of deadly violence in the east despite the disarmament of nearly 2,000 fighters and the gradual completion of the latest electoral cycle, the Security Council heard.

Illustrating the current fragility, the top UN official in the country, Valentine Rugwabiza, highlighted an attack on 30 June by different armed groups on Am-Dafock, bordering Sudan, which killed civilians, members of national security forces, displaced 17,000 civilians and injured six UN peacekeepers.

However, without peacekeeping mission MINUSCA’s rapid response, she said, attacks in the border area with Chad and Sudan would have resulted in significantly more fatalities and State authority could not have been restored after only five days of control by the armed group, whose fighters retreated across the border into Sudan.

“In this regard, I plead with the council, as it prepares to renew MINUSCA’s mandate, to maintain MINUSCA with adequate force levels and capabilities during the critical consolidation phase ,” she stressed.

While Bangui consolidates its authority and continues disarming rebel groups, violence is multiplying in the east, driven in part by the war in Sudan that is complicating plans for a gradual MINUSCA troop drawdown, Ms. Rugwabiza said.

The situation in the northeast and southeast remained particularly worrying, notably around mining sites and along the corridors traditionally used by pastoral farmers – often the source of community tensions.

In the southeast, 26 serious incidents were recorded, attributed to suspected members of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA – a long-established armed group of Ugandan origin – between June and September.
They included reports of rapes and sexual slavery and the abduction of 68 civilians, around 40 of them children.
At the same time, the Azandé Ani Kpi Gbé (AAKG) militia continues to threaten local populations.
articles.lede: The UN warned on Tuesday against a premature withdrawal of its peacekeepers as the war in Sudan spills over into the Central African Republic (CAR).

articles.title: AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must.
articles.description: AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must establish rules on autonomous weapons.
paragraphs: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed at extraordinary speed, prompting warnings from within the technology industry itself that advances may be outpacing our ability to understand and control its risks. Nowhere are the stakes higher than in armed conflict. As militaries increasingly explore the integration of AI into weapons and military decision-making, technological capability can easily be mistaken for inevitability: if a system can be built, the assumption follows that it will eventually be deployed. History suggests otherwise. States have made choices before about which technologies of warfare to prohibit, constrain or refrain from using – and they face such a choice again today.

In this post, ICRC Director of International Law, Movement and Partnerships Cordula Droege argues that abstract debates about the need to address the risks of AI should not distract from a concrete and achievable task already before states: establishing legally binding rules on autonomous weapon systems (AWS), including those incorporating AI. Drawing on the realities of deploying complex technologies in the unpredictable conditions of armed conflict, she explains why technical safeguards alone cannot resolve the humanitarian, legal and ethical concerns raised when weapons select and apply force without human intervention. Ahead of the Seventh Review Conference of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in November, she calls on states to turn more than a decade of work into clear prohibitions and restrictions on AWS, while there is still time to decide what role machines and algorithms should play in war.

Last month, American technology company CEOs made the case for somewhat slowing down the development of AI. Not for the first time, they clearly warned that the technology may be advancing faster than our ability to understand its consequences and put appropriate safeguards in place.

One week earlier, in the early hours of Saturday 5 September, in Geneva, the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons’ Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (CCW GGE on LAWS) closed its final session after three years of work.

On the face of it, these events concern quite different questions. One is about the pace of AI development, the other about international rules for weapons. But the two are connected. Trends indicate a push to integrate more complex algorithms into weapons, to increase their autonomy. The risks posed by AI – and especially the risks flagged in recent discussions that AI escapes the prediction of those who launch it – are perhaps the most consequential when it is integrated into weapons that can directly affect whether people live or die.

Both events therefore concern the question of whether the international community will act effectively to prevent potentially catastrophic harm from AI, or delay and be left to witness it once it occurs. At the recent UN Security Council meeting on 23 September, calls were made for “governance”, “frameworks” and “norm-setting”. These are welcome, but if they stay at this level of generality such calls will have no impact in reducing the suffering of people living through armed conflicts.
articles.lede: AI will not set its own limits in warfare. States must establish rules on autonomous weapons.

articles.description: The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism) warmly congratulates Judge Navi Pillay on receiving the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In her long and distinguished career, Judge Pillay served as Judge and President of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR).
paragraphs: During her 8-year tenure (1995-2003) at the ICTR, Judge Pillay played a critical role in the early formation of the Tribunal and the interpretation and application of international criminal law. She was elected in 1995 as one of the Tribunal’s first six judges, and its only woman judge during its first four years. She served as the ICTR’s second President from 1999 to 2003, which coincided with a period of rapid expansion and increased productivity. Notably, she played an essential role as a judge in the conduct and completion of seven trial proceedings. In particular, her work as a member of the bench on the Jean-Paul Akayesu case established that rape and other forms of sexual violence could amount to genocidal conduct. She participated in the landmark conviction and sentencing of Jean Kambanda, the former Prime Minister of Rwanda, the first head of government held accountable for genocide and crimes against humanity. Judge Pillay also presided over the Ferdinand Nahimana et al. trial which held the Rwandan media, both radio and print, responsible for fomenting ethnic hatred, genocide, and other international crimes.

The Mechanism’s President, Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, praised Judge Pillay as a “trailblazer in international criminal justice, who broke barriers as a woman judge and President of the ICTR, helping to shape a legacy of courage, integrity, and principled leadership. Her contributions continue to inspire generations of jurists and reaffirm the vital role of justice in upholding human dignity and lasting peace”.

The International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals (Mechanism) was established by UN Security Council Resolution 1966 (2010) to complete the remaining work of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia after the completion of their respective mandates. The Mechanism has two branches, one in Arusha, Tanzania, and one in The Hague, Netherlands.

Influencer, gamer, soldier, spy: the online era of child recruitment and its implications in international law (Part II)
articles.description: Online child recruitment is entering the digital age. From gaming to social media, discover how technology is changing the way children are drawn into armed conflict.
paragraphs: As social media and gaming platforms create new interfaces between tech-savvy children and armed actors, new questions should be asked regarding how the law prohibiting child recruitment and use in hostilities can be promoted and enforced online.

In this two-part post, ICRC Advisers Vanessa Murphy, Siobhan Sparkes McNamara, and Tilman Rodenhäuser consider how the digital environment is transforming more traditional forms of child recruitment, give a rough typology of related trends in the information and communications (ICT) environment, identify the relevant international law, and propose recommendations to improve compliance with these laws in the digital age.

In recent years, states have expressed concern about the use of ICTs for the recruitment of children into armed forces and armed groups, and their use in hostilities. Such acts are subject to widely-applicable international legal obligations, and this law applies online as well as offline: today, there is general agreement that “IHL rules and principles … serve to protect civilian populations and other protected persons and objects, including against the risks arising from ICT activities”, and that “children must not be allowed to take part in hostilities during armed conflict, including through ICT activities”.

But the intricacy of the rules governing child recruitment and use in hostilities is sometimes underestimated. In the second part of this post, we present some of the most relevant provisions and encourage states to take a range of measures to improve compliance with them.

Since the Geneva Conventions were adopted in 1949, international law has developed in bursts to advance the protection of children in armed conflict. Numerous treaties articulate in one way or another the general rule that these children are entitled to special respect and protection. This universal concern has birthed a more elaborate body of law to keep children away from the primary purveyors of violence in wartime – armed forces and armed groups.

Most states are bound by more than one of the following instruments governing child recruitment and use in hostilities, and all states are bound by at least one. When more than one norm applies to a given set of facts, the rules apply concurrently, meaning that the highest standard must be complied with. For example, many states are bound by prohibitions on child recruitment under the age of 15 ( API Art. 77.2, APII Art. 4.3.c, CRC Art. 38) as well as the higher age of 18 ( OPAC Art. 2 and declaration under Art. 3.2, ACRWC Art. 22.2 ). In such cases, a state must abide by the age 18 standard.

The Optional Protocol on the Protection of Children in Armed Conflict (OPAC). The 173 States Parties to OPAC are prohibited from unlawfully recruiting children to their own armed forces, including using online means, in line with the specifications in OPAC Articles 2 and 3. They must also “ take all feasible measures to prevent” the recruitment or use in hostilities of persons under 18 by non-state armed groups, “ including the adoption of legal measures necessary to prohibit and criminalize such practices” (Art. 4.2). For their part, non-state armed groups are prohibited from recruiting or using in hostilities anyone under 18 (Art. 4.1). Finally, under Article 6.1 and 6.2, States Parties must take “ all necessary legal, administrative and other measures to ensure the effective implementation and enforcement of the provisions of the present Protocol within its jurisdiction ”.
